The network (AMF) may detect and start performing S-NSSAI based congestion control when one or more **S-NSSAI congestion criteria**, as specified in 3GPP TS 23.501 [8], are met.

**Handling of missing DNN/S-NSSAI for a non-emergency PDU session:**

- **If the UE does not provide a DNN** for a non-emergency PDU session, then the network uses the **selected DNN**.

- **If the UE does not provide an S-NSSAI** for a non-emergency PDU session, then the network uses the **selected S-NSSAI**.

*(Note: In the AMF-specific context of Clause 5.3.11, this is stated slightly more precisely — the AMF uses the selected DNN/S-NSSAI, or alternatively the DNN/S-NSSAI associated with the PDU session corresponding to the 5GSM procedure, if applicable.)*
results.evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.3.11, Handling of S-NSSAI based congestion control

results.question: How does the UE determine the PLMN scope for applying timer T3584 when it receives a 5GSM congestion re-attempt indicator IE with the ABO bit set to 'The back-off timer is applied in all PLMNs' along with cause #67?
results.reference: If the 5GSM congestion re-attempt indicator IE with the ABO bit set to 'The back-off timer is applied in all PLMNs' is included in the 5GSM message with cause value #67 'insufficient resources for specific slice and DNN', then the UE applies timer T3584 for all PLMNs. Otherwise, the UE applies timer T3584 only for the registered PLMN.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.2.8, Handling of S-NSSAI based congestion control
results.model_answer:
Based on the specification, when the UE receives cause #67 "insufficient resources for specific slice and DNN" together with the Back-off timer value IE, the scope of T3584 (i.e., whether it applies only to the registered PLMN or to **all PLMNs**) is determined specifically by the **5GSM congestion re-attempt indicator IE's ABO bit**, not by the Re-attempt indicator IE (which is explicitly ignored for this cause).

The rule is:

- **If** the 5GSM congestion re-attempt indicator IE is included in the rejecting message (e.g., PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REJECT, PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REJECT, or PDU SESSION RELEASE COMMAND) **with the 5GSM cause value #67**, **and** its **ABO bit is set to "The back-off timer is applied in all PLMNs"**, then the UE **shall apply timer T3584 for all PLMNs**.
- **Otherwise** (i.e., if the 5GSM congestion re-attempt indicator IE is absent, or present but the ABO bit is not set to that value), the UE **shall apply timer T3584 only for the registered PLMN**.

This determination is made **independently of the Re-attempt indicator IE**, which the UE is instructed to ignore entirely when cause #67 is received with the Back-off timer value IE — the ABO bit in the 5GSM congestion re-attempt indicator IE is the sole determinant of PLMN scope in this case.

**Consequence on association:** When the timer is set to apply for all PLMNs, T3584 becomes associated with the **[mapped S-NSSAI, DNN]** combination of the PDU session (rather than the S-NSSAI as provided by the UE), and it only starts once the UE is actually registered in a VPLMN with the S-NSSAI provided during PDU session establishment. This "all PLMNs" scope also means that when the timer is stopped or restarted (e.g., upon receiving a new Back-off timer value for the same [S-NSSAI, DNN] combination), both the "for all PLMNs" instance and any "for the registered PLMN" instance of T3584 are stopped together, since the specification states the timer "to be stopped includes the timer T3584 applied for all the PLMNs, if running, and the timer T3584 applied for the registered PLMN, if running."

If the timer scope is instead limited to the registered PLMN (ABO bit not set to "all PLMNs" or the IE not included), then a PLMN change does **not** automatically clear the restriction — the UE does not stop T3584 upon PLMN or inter-system change — but the UE **is** allowed to send a new PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST for the same S-NSSAI/DNN combination in a **new** PLMN if T3584 is not running/deactivated for that combination in the new PLMN (this per-PLMN reset behavior does not apply if the "all PLMNs" scope was set, since in that case the restriction follows the UE across PLMNs).

results.question: When timer T3585 is running or deactivated for all PLMNs and is associated with no S-NSSAI, what procedures is the UE not allowed to initiate, and what are the exceptions?
results.reference: The UE is not allowed to initiate the PDU session establishment procedure, PDU session modification procedure, or NAS transport procedure for sending CIoT user data for no S-NSSAI in any PLMN. The exceptions are if the UE is configured for high priority access in selected PLMN or needs to report a change of 3GPP PS data off UE status.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.2.8, Handling of S-NSSAI based congestion control
results.model_answer:
When T3585 is running or deactivated for **all PLMNs** and associated with **no S-NSSAI**, the UE is **not allowed to initiate**, for "no S-NSSAI" **in any PLMN**:

a) PDU session establishment procedure
b) PDU session modification procedure
c) NAS transport procedure for sending CIoT user data

**Exceptions** — the UE is allowed to initiate these procedures if:
- the UE is configured for **high priority access in the selected PLMN**, or
- the initiation is **to report a change of 3GPP PS data off UE status**

results.question: In a VPLMN, what restriction applies to a UE regarding the initiation of certain procedures when the mapped S-NSSAI provided during PDU session establishment matches the S-NSSAI associated with a running timer T3585?
results.reference: A UE registered in a VPLMN is not allowed to initiate the PDU session establishment procedure, PDU session modification procedure, or NAS transport procedure for sending CIoT user data when the mapped S-NSSAI provided during PDU session establishment is the same as the S-NSSAI associated with timer T3585. The exceptions are if the UE is configured for high priority access in selected PLMN or needs to report a change of 3GPP PS data off UE status.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.2.8, Handling of S-NSSAI based congestion control
results.model_answer:
Based on clause 6.2.8, when timer **T3585 is running or is deactivated for all the PLMNs** and is associated with an S-NSSAI other than "no S-NSSAI," a UE registered in a **VPLMN** is **not allowed to initiate**:

1. the **PDU session establishment procedure**;
2. the **PDU session modification procedure**; or
3. the **NAS transport procedure for sending CIoT user data**

when the **mapped S-NSSAI** provided by the UE during the PDU session establishment is the **same** as the S-NSSAI associated with timer T3585.

This restriction does **not** apply if the UE is a **UE configured for high priority access in the selected PLMN**, or if the procedure is being used **to report a change of 3GPP PS data off UE status** — these are the two explicit exceptions carved out in the specification.

results.question: Under what two conditions would the network include the T3448 value IE?
results.reference: The network includes the T3448 value IE when both of the following conditions are met: congestion control for transport of user data via the control plane is active, and the UE supports the control plane CIoT 5GS optimizations.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.7.29, T3448 value
results.model_answer:
Based on the context provided, the network includes the **T3448 value IE** under two conditions:

1. **General congestion control activation (Clause [1] / [2] / [5] / [6]):**
 The network may include the T3448 value IE in a REGISTRATION ACCEPT, SERVICE ACCEPT, or SERVICE REJECT message if:
 - the UE has indicated support for **control plane CIoT 5GS optimizations**, and
 - the network decides to **activate congestion control** for transport of user data via the control plane.

2. **Specific case during CONTROL PLANE SERVICE REQUEST handling with uplink data (Clause [7] / [8]):**
 The AMF shall send a SERVICE ACCEPT message with the T3448 value IE included if, upon receipt of a CONTROL PLANE SERVICE REQUEST message with uplink data:
 - the DDX field of the Release assistance indication IE or the DDX field of the CIoT small data container IE is set to "No further uplink and no further downlink data transmission subsequent to the uplink data transmission is expected", **and**
 - the AMF decides to **forward the uplink data** piggybacked in the CONTROL PLANE SERVICE REQUEST message, **and**
 - the AMF decides to **activate congestion control** for transport of user data via the control plane.

In short:
- **Condition 1** — the UE supports CP CIoT 5GS optimizations *and* the network activates control-plane data congestion control (general case, applicable across REGISTRATION ACCEPT/SERVICE ACCEPT/SERVICE REJECT).
- **Condition 2** — a more specific triggering scenario tied to the CONTROL PLANE SERVICE REQUEST procedure, where uplink data is forwarded and no further uplink/downlink transmission is expected, combined with the AMF's decision to activate congestion control.

results.question: How does the activation of congestion control for user data transport via the control plane relate to the inclusion of the T3448 value IE?
results.reference: The activation of congestion control for transport of user data via the control plane is one of the necessary conditions that prompts the network to include the T3448 value IE, provided the UE also supports the required optimizations.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.7.29, T3448 value
results.model_answer:
The relationship is conditional and one‑directional: activation of the congestion control feature is a **necessary pre‑condition** for the network to include the T3448 value IE, but it does not by itself guarantee inclusion.

- **Why the link exists:** Timer T3448 is the mechanism by which the network throttles ("backs off") UE‑initiated control‑plane data transport when congestion control for that transport is active (clauses [1]/[4]). The T3448 value IE is simply the carrier of that timer's value in NAS messages.

- **Conditions for inclusion:** Per clauses [2], [3], [5] and [8] (8.2.7.29, 8.2.18.5, 8.2.17.6), the network **may** include the T3448 value IE in REGISTRATION ACCEPT, SERVICE ACCEPT or SERVICE REJECT **only if**:
  1. congestion control for transport of user data via the control plane **is active**, **and**
  2. the UE **supports** control‑plane CIoT 5GS optimizations.

  Both conditions must hold; activation alone (without UE support) does not lead to inclusion.

- **Not automatic/mandatory:** Even when both conditions are satisfied, inclusion is optional ("may include") — the network decides per UE, choosing timer values to avoid synchronized timeouts across UEs ([1]/[4]).

- **De-activation behavior:** Conversely, when the AMF decides to **deactivate** congestion control, it must delete the stored per‑UE back‑off time and **must not** include the T3448 value IE in the SERVICE ACCEPT message ([6]/[7]). Similarly, sending REGISTRATION ACCEPT/SERVICE ACCEPT **without** the T3448 value IE is the explicit signal used to **stop** a running T3448 timer in the UE.

- **UE-side handling reinforces this coupling:** If the IE is present with a non-zero/non-deactivated value, the UE (re)starts T3448 with that value. If present but indicating zero/deactivated, the UE ignores it (treats as not present). If absent while T3448 is running (in the CONTROL PLANE SERVICE REQUEST-triggered SERVICE ACCEPT case), the UE stops T3448.

**In summary:** Congestion control activation (plus UE CIoT-CP support) is the gating condition that permits the network to include T3448; the actual inclusion/exclusion of the IE is then used dynamically to start, refresh, or stop the timer, effectively signaling the current congestion-control state to the UE.

results.question: What role does UE support for control plane CIoT 5GS optimizations play in the network's decision to include the T3448 value IE?
results.reference: UE support for control plane CIoT 5GS optimizations is a prerequisite condition; the network will only include the T3448 value IE if the UE has this capability, and only when congestion control for user data transport via the control plane is also active.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.7.29, T3448 value
results.model_answer:
Based on clauses [1], [4], [5], and [6], UE support for control plane CIoT 5GS optimizations is a **precondition/gating factor** for the network including the T3448 value IE — it is not sufficient on its own, but it is necessary.

Specifically:

1. **Necessary condition**: The network may include the T3448 value IE only **if the UE supports control plane CIoT 5GS optimizations AND congestion control for transport of user data via the control plane is active** (clauses [4], [5], [6]). Both conditions must hold together — support alone does not trigger inclusion.

2. **Rationale tied to relevance**: Timer T3448 exists specifically to throttle/back-off *control-plane* transport of user data (per [1]). If a UE does not support control plane CIoT 5GS optimizations, it has no capability to use the control-plane data transport path in the first place, so there would be no purpose in signaling a control-plane data back-off timer to it. Hence UE support acts as an applicability filter — the network would not include T3448 value IE for a UE that cannot use this optimization, even if congestion control is active, since the timer is meaningless for a UE incapable of the corresponding data transfer mode.

3. **Network still has discretion**: Even when the UE supports control plane CIoT 5GS optimizations, inclusion of T3448 value IE is not mandatory — the network "may" include it, based on its own decision to activate congestion control for control-plane user data transport (per [1] and [7]/[8], where the AMF decides whether to activate congestion control and only then sends the T3448 value IE in SERVICE ACCEPT/REGISTRATION ACCEPT/SERVICE REJECT).

In summary: **UE support for control plane CIoT 5GS optimizations is a necessary enabling condition** — without it, the network shall not include the T3448 value IE, since the timer is only meaningful for a UE that can use control-plane data transport. Whether the network actually includes the IE depends additionally on whether it has decided to activate congestion control for control-plane user data transport at that time.

results.question: Under what conditions should a UE stop timer T3396 associated with no DNN upon receiving a PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND message?
results.reference: The UE should stop the timer T3396 associated with no DNN if it is running when the UE did not provide a DNN during the PDU session establishment and the request type was different from both 'initial emergency request' and 'existing emergency PDU session'. It must not stop this timer if the message was received for an emergency PDU session.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.2.3, Network-requested PDU session modification procedure accepted by the UE
results.model_answer:
Based on TS 24.501, **T3396 associated with no DNN** is stopped upon receipt of a PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND (i.e., an accepted PDU session modification, per subclause 6.3.2.3, which parallels the T3396 handling shown in the PDU SESSION AUTHENTICATION COMMAND clause [5]/[6]) when **all** of the following conditions hold:

1. **No DNN was provided by the UE** during the establishment of the PDU session to which the modification applies (i.e., the timer instance in question is the one associated with "no DNN", as opposed to a DNN-specific T3396 instance).

2. **Timer T3396 (associated with no DNN) is actually running** at the time the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND is received (there is nothing to stop otherwise).

3. The PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND is received **for a PDU session that was established without a DNN**, and that PDU session's request type was **different from "initial emergency request"** and **different from "existing emergency PDU session"** — i.e., it is **not an emergency PDU session**.
   - Conversely, if the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND was received for an **emergency PDU session**, the UE shall **not** stop the T3396 timer associated with no DNN (the no-DNN emergency exception is preserved consistently across the analogous PDU SESSION RELEASE COMMAND/PDU SESSION AUTHENTICATION COMMAND handling described in the context).

4. This stopping applies to **both** the T3396 instance applied for all PLMNs (if running) and the T3396 instance applied for the registered PLMN (if running) — i.e., all applicable "no DNN" T3396 instances are stopped together.

**Summary condition:** The UE stops T3396 associated with no DNN upon receiving a PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND message for a non-emergency PDU session that was established without a DNN, provided that timer instance is currently running (covering both the all-PLMNs and registered-PLMN variants); it must not be stopped if the PDU session is an emergency PDU session.

results.question: How does the UE determine which timer T3584 to stop when it receives a PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND message and it provided a DNN but no S-NSSAI during session establishment?
results.reference: The UE stops timer T3584 if it is running for the same [no S-NSSAI, DNN] combination that was provided by the UE during the PDU session establishment.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.2.3, Network-requested PDU session modification procedure accepted by the UE
results.model_answer:
When the UE provided a **DNN but no S-NSSAI** during PDU session establishment, receipt of a PDU SESSION AUTHENTICATION/MODIFICATION-type stopping trigger (as described for T3584 handling, e.g. in the PDU SESSION AUTHENTICATION COMMAND procedure and analogously for a PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND) causes the UE to stop the timer T3584 associated with the **[no S-NSSAI, DNN] combination** — i.e., the combination formed using "no S-NSSAI" (since none was provided) and the DNN that was actually provided by the UE for that PDU session.

This follows the general pattern established in the specification: T3584 is always keyed to a **[S-NSSAI (or no S-NSSAI), DNN (or no DNN)] combination**, matching exactly what the UE provided during the PDU session establishment request. Since:

- An S-NSSAI **was not** provided → the "S-NSSAI" slot of the combination is **no S-NSSAI**
- A DNN **was** provided → the "DNN" slot of the combination is the **actual DNN**

the UE therefore identifies and stops the T3584 instance tied to the **[no S-NSSAI, DNN]** combination — including both the variant of T3584 applied for all PLMNs (if running) and the variant applied for the registered PLMN (if running).

This is consistent with how the UE stops T3584 in other contexts (e.g., on receipt of a PDU SESSION AUTHENTICATION COMMAND, per [7]/[8]): "If the UE provided a DNN but did not provide an S-NSSAI during the PDU session establishment, the UE shall stop timer T3584, if it is running for the same **[no S-NSSAI, DNN]** combination provided by the UE." The same mapping logic (DNN/no-DNN and S-NSSAI/no-S-NSSAI combination matching what was originally sent) applies when the stopping trigger is a PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND message for that same [no S-NSSAI, DNN] combination.

results.question: What action must the UE take regarding a Port management information container when sending a PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMPLETE message?
results.reference: If a port management information container needs to be delivered, the UE must include a Port management information container IE in the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMPLETE message.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.2.3, Network-requested PDU session modification procedure accepted by the UE
results.model_answer:
If a port management information container needs to be delivered, the UE shall include a **Port management information container IE** in the **PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMPLETE** message (per handling described in 3GPP TS 23.501 and TS 23.502).

This is consistent with clause 8.3.7.11, which specifies that the Port management information container IE "shall be included when the UE needs to convey a port management information container" — confirming the inclusion is conditional on there being a container to deliver, not mandatory in every PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMPLETE message.
results.evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.15.4, User plane node management

results.question: What are the SMF's actions upon receiving a PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMPLETE message for a PDU session using SSC mode 3 where the command included cause #39?
results.reference: The SMF must stop timer T3591, consider the PDU session as modified, and start timer T3593. The value for T3593 is the PDU Session Address Lifetime value if it was sent in the command, otherwise a default value is used.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.2.3, Network-requested PDU session modification procedure accepted by the UE
results.model_answer:
Upon receipt of the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMPLETE message, the SMF shall:

1. **Stop timer T3591** and consider the PDU session as modified.

2. Since the selected SSC mode of the PDU session is **"SSC mode 3"** and the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND message included 5GSM cause #39 "reactivation requested", the SMF shall **start timer T3593**:
   - If the PDU Session Address Lifetime value was sent to the UE in the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND message, timer T3593 shall be started with **that same value**.
   - Otherwise, timer T3593 shall be started with a **default value**.

3. If the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMPLETE message contains a **Port management information container IE**, the SMF shall handle the contents of that IE as specified in 3GPP TS 23.501 and TS 23.502.
results.evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.2.3, Network-requested PDU session modification procedure accepted by the UE

results.question: How does a UE operating in dual-registration mode maintain its contexts for 5GMM and EMM, and what is the general rule regarding coordination between these two management entities?
results.reference: The UE maintains independent contexts for 5GMM and EMM, including independent lists of equivalent PLMNs. Coordination between 5GMM and EMM is generally not needed, except as specified in specific subclauses.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.8.3, Dual-registration mode
results.model_answer:
Based on Clause 4.8.3, a UE operating in **dual-registration mode** (with both 5GMM and EMM enabled) maintains **independent contexts** for 5GMM and EMM. This independence explicitly includes maintaining **independent lists of equivalent PLMNs** for each entity.

**General rule on coordination:**

Coordination between 5GMM and EMM is **not needed** in dual-registration mode, except in three specific cases:

1. **Subclause 4.8.3 itself** – which defines the specific dual-registration mode behaviors (e.g., rules for using the same or an equivalent PLMN when registering in one mode after already being registered in the other, as described in points (c) and (d) of that clause).

2. **Subclause 5.1.5** – which addresses coordination of "SIM/USIM considered invalid" and "USIM considered invalid for 5GS services" across all mobility management entities (5GMM, EMM, GMM, MM), regardless of whether the UE operates in single- or dual-registration mode.

3. **Subclause 5.3.13A** – covering an additional specific coordination scenario.

This contrasts with **single-registration mode**, where the UE must maintain **one common registration** for 5GMM (3GPP access) and EMM, requiring active coordination between the two as detailed in subclauses 5.1.4.2 (with N26 interface) and 5.1.4.3 (without N26 interface).

In essence, dual-registration mode treats 5GMM and EMM as largely autonomous, independently-managed state machines, with the UE itself (via implementation-specific logic, as noted in NOTE1 and NOTE4 of Clause 4.8.3) responsible for reconciling registration states across N1 mode and S1 mode when necessary — rather than relying on mandated protocol-level coordination.

results.question: If a UE is registered only in N1 mode, what PLMN selection rules must it follow when attempting to register in S1 mode?
results.reference: The UE must use either the same PLMN to which it is registered in N1 mode, or an equivalent PLMN.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.8.3, Dual-registration mode
results.model_answer:
Based on Clause 4.8.3 (Dual-registration mode), if a UE is registered in N1 mode only, then for registration in S1 mode the UE shall use:

1. **The same PLMN** to which it is registered in N1 mode; **or**
2. **An equivalent PLMN** (i.e., a PLMN from the equivalent PLMN list associated with its N1 mode registration)

This ensures consistency between the UE's registrations across the two modes when operating in dual-registration mode, since the UE maintains independent 5GMM and EMM contexts (including independent equivalent PLMN lists) but must still align the PLMN used for S1 mode registration with the one already established in N1 mode (or an equivalent thereof).

results.question: How can a UE transfer active PDN connections from S1 mode to N1 mode after successfully registering in N1 mode, and what is the subsequent impact on its EMM state if all connections are transferred?
results.reference: The UE can transfer one or more active PDN connections by initiating the PDU session establishment procedure with request type set to 'existing PDU session'. If all PDN connections are transferred to 5GS, the UE may stay in EMM-REGISTERED if the MME supports it without a PDN connection; otherwise, it must enter EMM-DEREGISTERED.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.8.3, Dual-registration mode
results.model_answer:
Based on Clause 4.8.3 (Dual-registration mode):

**Transfer mechanism:**
After the UE has successfully registered in N1 mode, it may transfer one or more active PDN connections from S1 mode to N1 mode by initiating the **PDU session establishment procedure** with the **request type set to "existing PDU session"**. It is up to UE implementation to determine which specific active PDN connection(s) are transferred (NOTE3).

**Impact on EMM state once all PDN connections are transferred:**

- **If the MME supports EMM-REGISTERED without PDN connection:** the UE may remain in state **EMM-REGISTERED**, even though it no longer has any PDN connections in S1 mode.

- **If the MME does not support EMM-REGISTERED without PDN connection:** the UE **shall enter state EMM-DEREGISTERED** upon transferring all its PDN connections to the 5GS, since maintaining EMM-REGISTERED without any PDN connection is not supported in that case.

Thus, the outcome hinges on MME capability: support for "EMM-REGISTERED without PDN connection" allows the UE to stay registered in S1 mode (dual registration) even with no active PDN connections there, whereas its absence forces the UE to deregister from EMM once it has moved all its connectivity to N1 mode.

results.question: What triggers the mandatory inclusion of the NID IE based on the 5GS mobile identity?
results.reference: The trigger is a mismatch between the SNPN that allocated the 5G-GUTI contained within the 5GS mobile identity IE and the SNPN to which the registration procedure is being performed.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.6.36, NID
results.model_answer:
The NID IE must be included when the 5G-GUTI carried in the 5GS mobile identity IE was assigned by an SNPN **other than** the SNPN the UE is currently registering with.

This ties directly to clause 5.5.1.2.2, which states that if the UE is registering with an SNPN and holds a valid 5G-GUTI previously assigned by *any other SNPN* (not the one it's currently registering with), and the UE is not performing initial registration for onboarding services, then:

- the UE shall indicate that 5G-GUTI in the 5GS mobile identity IE, **and**
- shall additionally include the NID of that other SNPN in the NID IE.

So the trigger is specifically: **the 5G-GUTI included in the 5GS mobile identity IE originates from a different SNPN than the one the UE is registering with** — in that case, the NID of the originating (other) SNPN must be included so the network can identify which SNPN issued that 5G-GUTI.

results.question: What actions should the AMF take upon the fifth expiry of timer T3560 during an EAP-based primary authentication and key agreement procedure?
results.reference: The AMF shall abort the EAP-based primary authentication and key agreement procedure and any ongoing 5GMM specific procedure, and release the N1 NAS signalling connection.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.1.2.4.4, Abnormal cases on the network side
results.model_answer:
Upon the **fifth expiry** of timer T3560 during the EAP-based primary authentication and key agreement procedure, the AMF shall:

1. **Abort** the EAP based primary authentication and key agreement procedure;
2. **Abort** any ongoing 5GMM specific procedure; and
3. **Release** the N1 NAS signalling connection.

(Note: This occurs after the AMF has already retransmitted the AUTHENTICATION REQUEST message four times, resetting and restarting T3560 on each of the first four expiries.)

results.question: How does the AMF handle the scenario where the AUTHENTICATION REQUEST message cannot be delivered due to an intra AMF handover, and the target TA is included in the TAI list?
results.reference: Upon successful completion of the intra AMF handover, the AMF shall retransmit the AUTHENTICATION REQUEST message.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.1.2.4.4, Abnormal cases on the network side
results.model_answer: When the AUTHENTICATION REQUEST message could not be delivered because of an intra-AMF handover, and the target TA is part of the TAI list, the AMF waits for the handover to complete successfully. Upon successful completion of the intra-AMF handover, the AMF shall retransmit the AUTHENTICATION REQUEST message to the UE.

results.question: What is the procedure for the AMF when a failure of the handover procedure is reported by the lower layer and the N1 NAS signalling connection still exists?
results.reference: The AMF shall retransmit the AUTHENTICATION REQUEST message.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.1.2.4.4, Abnormal cases on the network side
results.model_answer:
When the lower layer reports a handover failure and the N1 NAS signalling connection still exists, the AMF shall retransmit the message associated with the ongoing procedure that was pending delivery. This applies consistently across the relevant NAS procedures:

- **EAP-based / 5G AKA based primary authentication and key agreement procedure**: the AMF shall retransmit the **AUTHENTICATION REQUEST** message.
- **Security mode control procedure**: the AMF shall retransmit the **SECURITY MODE COMMAND** message.
- **Network slice-specific authentication and authorization procedure**: the AMF shall retransmit the **NETWORK SLICE-SPECIFIC AUTHENTICATION COMMAND** message.

In each case, the retransmission upon handover failure (with the N1 NAS signalling connection still existing) is handled the same way regardless of whether the target TA/TAI is in the TAI list — the AMF simply retransmits the previously undelivered message, since the signalling connection to the UE is still available.

results.question: Upon the first expiry of timer T3560, what actions must the AMF perform regarding the AUTHENTICATION REQUEST message and timer T3560?
results.reference: The AMF shall retransmit the AUTHENTICATION REQUEST message and shall reset and start timer T3560.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.1.2.4.4, Abnormal cases on the network side
results.model_answer:
Upon the **first expiry** of timer T3560, the AMF shall:

1. **Retransmit** the AUTHENTICATION REQUEST message; and
2. **Reset and restart** timer T3560.

This retransmission process is repeated up to four times in total. If T3560 expires a **fifth** time, the AMF shall instead abort the authentication procedure (and any ongoing 5GMM specific procedure) and release the N1 NAS signalling connection, rather than retransmitting again.

results.question: What is the required action for both the UE and the network when encountering an unknown IE that is not marked for comprehension?
results.reference: Both shall ignore the unknown Information Element.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 7.6.1, IEIs unknown in the message
results.model_answer:
Based on Clause 7.6.1 ("IEIs unknown in the message"), when an unknown IE is encountered that is **not** encoded as "comprehension required":

**Both the UE and the network shall simply ignore the unknown IE.**

Specifically:
- **The UE** shall ignore all IEs unknown in a message which are not encoded as "comprehension required."
- **The network** shall take the same approach (i.e., also ignore such unknown IEs).

**Key distinction:** This behavior applies only to IEs that are unknown *and* not flagged as "comprehension required" per 3GPP TS 24.007. This is different from the handling described in Clause 7.5.1, where an unknown IE that *is* encoded as "comprehension required" triggers error-handling procedures (e.g., returning a STATUS message with cause #96 "invalid mandatory information," subject to the message-specific exceptions in subclause 7.5.3).

In short: no error indication, no status message, and no rejection procedure is triggered — the unknown, non-comprehension-required IE is simply discarded/ignored by both sides, and the rest of the message is processed normally.

results.question: What is the functional relationship between the two 5GMM modes and the N1 NAS signalling connection?
results.reference: The two 5GMM modes, IDLE and CONNECTED, are functionally defined by the absence or presence, respectively, of the N1 NAS signalling connection. The connection's establishment moves the UE to CONNECTED mode, while its release returns the UE to IDLE mode.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.3.1, 5GMM modes and N1 NAS signalling connection
results.model_answer:
# Relationship Between 5GMM Modes and the N1 NAS Signalling Connection

Based on the context provided (particularly clauses 4.4.2.5, 5.3.1.5, and 4.4.5), the N1 NAS signalling connection existence is what fundamentally distinguishes the two 5GMM modes, but the relationship is **not strictly binary** due to the CIoT suspend/resume mechanism. Here is the functional relationship:

## 1. Baseline Rule: Connection Presence Defines the Mode

- **5GMM-CONNECTED mode**: The UE has an active N1 NAS signalling connection to the AMF. This connection carries the NAS security context (once established) and allows immediate exchange of ciphered/integrity-protected NAS messages.
- **5GMM-IDLE mode**: No N1 NAS signalling connection exists (in the normal case), or if one existed, it has been released.

## 2. The Connection Is Established/Released, Triggering Mode Transitions

- Establishing a NAS signalling connection (e.g., via an initial NAS message from the UE) drives the transition **into 5GMM-CONNECTED mode**.
- Releasing the NAS signalling connection drives the transition **into 5GMM-IDLE mode** (normal idle, without suspend indication).

## 3. Exception: Suspend/Resume Decouples Mode from Connection (Clause 5.3.1.5)

This is the key nuance: when **user plane CIoT 5GS optimization** is used, the relationship is deliberately broken:

- Upon an **idle suspend indication** from lower layers, the UE/network enters **5GMM-IDLE mode with suspend indication** — but explicitly:
  - **shall NOT consider the N1 NAS signalling connection released**, and
  - **shall NOT consider the secure exchange of NAS messages terminated**.

This means the UE/AMF can be in **5GMM-IDLE mode** while the N1 NAS signalling connection (and its associated security context) is still logically "alive," just suspended at the AS/RRC layer.

- Upon **resume** (RRC connection resumed, or NGAP UE context resume request received), the UE/network transitions back to **5GMM-CONNECTED mode**, reusing the same (never-terminated) N1 NAS signalling connection and its already-established secure exchange of NAS messages — **without needing to re-establish security** from scratch.

## 4. Consequence for Security Context Continuity

Because the N1 NAS signalling connection (and secure exchange of NAS messages, clause 4.4.2.5/4.4.5) is preserved across suspend/resume cycles:
- Ciphering/integrity protection continues seamlessly upon resume, since the connection was never torn down — only suspended.
- This contrasts with a genuine connection release, which terminates the secure exchange of NAS messages (per 4.4.2.5), requiring re-establishment (via security mode control or re-verification with ngKSI/MAC) the next time a connection is created.

## Summary

| Scenario | 5GMM Mode | N1 Connection Status | Secure NAS Exchange |
|---|---|---|---|
| Normal connection active | CONNECTED | Established | Active |
| Normal connection released | IDLE | Released | Terminated |
| CIoT suspend | IDLE (with suspend indication) | **Not released** | **Not terminated** |
| CIoT resume | CONNECTED | Same connection reactivated | Continues unchanged |

**In essence**: the N1 NAS signalling connection's lifecycle *normally* maps one-to-one with the 5GMM mode transitions (CONNECTED ↔ IDLE), but the CIoT suspend/resume feature introduces a special IDLE sub-state ("IDLE with suspend indication") where the connection and its security context persist logically despite the UE being in IDLE mode — decoupling the *mode* from the *connection's actual existence* in that specific case.
results.evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.3, General on elementary 5GMM procedures

results.question: What is the purpose of the network-requested PDU session modification procedure regarding header compression?
results.reference: The procedure enables the network to re-negotiate the header compression configuration associated with a PDU session.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.2.1, General
results.model_answer:
The purpose, with respect to header compression, is **to enable the network to re-negotiate the header compression configuration associated with a PDU session**.

This is one of several purposes served by the network-requested PDU session modification procedure (as stated in Clause 6.3.2.1), alongside modifying the PDU session, conveying port management information, triggering EAS rediscovery, providing updated DNS/ECS information, MBS-related updates, ATSSS parameter updates, and service-level AA/C2 authorization results.

More specifically, per Clause 6.3.2.2, this re-negotiation works as follows:

- **IP header compression**: If control plane CIoT 5GS optimization is enabled for the PDU session, and the IP header compression configuration IE was included by the UE in the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST or PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REQUEST message, and the SMF supports both control plane CIoT 5GS optimization and IP header compression for it, then the SMF **may** include the IP header compression configuration IE in the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND message to re-negotiate the IP header compression configuration for that PDU session.

- **Ethernet header compression**: Similarly, if control plane CIoT 5GS optimization is enabled and the Ethernet header compression configuration IE was included by the UE, and the SMF supports control plane CIoT 5GS optimization and Ethernet header compression for it, the SMF **may** include the Ethernet header compression configuration IE in the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND message to re-configure the Ethernet header compression configuration for that PDU session.
results.evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.2.16, Handling of header compression for control plane CIoT optimizations

results.question: What condition must be met for an SMF supporting NB-N1 mode to apply the specific timer calculation rule?
results.reference: The SMF must be performing NAS signalling with a UE that is using NB-N1 mode.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.18, 5GS session management in NB-N1 mode
results.model_answer: The SMF must be **performing NAS signalling with a UE that is using NB-N1 mode** — in that case, per clause 4.18, the SMF (which must itself support NB-N1 mode) shall calculate the value of the applicable NAS timer indicated in table 10.3.2 by adding 180s to it.

results.question: How does the AMF indicate that general NAS level mobility management congestion control is currently active?
results.reference: The AMF indicates this by including the T3346 value information element in a NAS message.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.18.3, T3346 value
results.model_answer:
The AMF indicates that general NAS level mobility management congestion control is active by **including the T3346 value IE in the applicable 5GMM reject message** sent to the UE.

Specifically, per Clause 5.3.9 (and mirrored in [1]–[4], [8]): "When general NAS level congestion control is active, the AMF may include a value for the mobility management back-off timer T3346 in the reject messages." This is an optional/conditional IE — the AMF *may* include it specifically when congestion control is active, meaning the presence of the T3346 value IE in the reject message (e.g., in REGISTRATION REJECT, SERVICE REJECT, or other 5GMM reject messages referenced in clauses 8.2.9.2, 8.2.14.3, 8.2.18.3) serves as the implicit signal to the UE that congestion control is currently active at the AMF.

The UE, upon receiving this T3346 value IE in a 5GMM reject message, starts timer T3346 with the received value — this timer start action on the UE side reflects that the network has activated congestion control and is deferring the rejected request type.

So there is no separate explicit "congestion active" flag/IE — the **conditional inclusion of the T3346 value IE itself** in the reject message is the indicator, since this IE's presence is explicitly tied to the condition "the AMF may include this IE when the general NAS level mobility management congestion control is active."

results.question: What are the two primary purposes of the service-level authentication and authorization procedure when establishing a PDU session?
results.reference: The procedure is used to authenticate the upper layers of the UE and to authorize the upper layers of the UE when establishing the PDU session.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.1A, Service-level authentication and authorization procedure
results.model_answer:
Based on Clause 6.3.1A, when establishing a PDU session, the service-level authentication and authorization (service-level-AA) procedure exists to enable the DN (using NEF services) to:

1. **Authenticate the upper layers of the UE**
2. **Authorize the upper layers of the UE**

(Both can also be performed together, i.e., "both of the above" — but the two primary distinct purposes during PDU session establishment are authentication and authorization. A separate, third purpose — re-authentication — applies only *after* the PDU session has already been established, not during establishment.)
results.evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.1A, Service-level authentication and authorization procedure

results.question: Under what condition is the service-level authentication and authorization procedure explicitly prohibited?
results.reference: The procedure shall not be performed during or after the UE-requested PDU session establishment procedure establishing an emergency PDU session.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.1A, Service-level authentication and authorization procedure
results.model_answer:
The procedure **shall not** be performed during or after the UE-requested PDU session establishment procedure that establishes an **emergency PDU session**.

As stated in the context: "The service-level authentication and authorization procedure can be performed only during or after the UE-requested PDU session procedure establishing a non-emergency PDU session. The service-level authentication and authorization procedure shall not be performed during or after the UE-requested PDU session establishment procedure establishing an emergency PDU session."

results.question: How is a successful service-level-AA response delivered to the UE when the procedure is performed for re-authentication on an established PDU session?
results.reference: The successful service-level-AA response is transported from the network to the UE as part of the network-requested PDU session modification procedure in the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND message.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.1A, Service-level authentication and authorization procedure
results.model_answer:
Based on clause 6.3.1A, when the service-level authentication and authorization procedure is performed **for re-authentication** on an already-established PDU session, and the service-level-AA procedure completes **successfully**, the service-level-AA response is **not** sent via a standalone message — instead it is transported from the network to the UE **as part of the network-requested PDU session modification procedure, carried within the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND message**.

This contrasts with:
- The case where the re-authentication completes **unsuccessfully**, in which case the response is instead carried in the **PDU SESSION RELEASE COMMAND message** (as part of the network-requested PDU session release procedure), and
- The case where the service-level-AA procedure is performed **during initial PDU session establishment**, where success/failure responses are carried in the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT ACCEPT/REJECT messages respectively.

results.question: What does the UE do with a service-level-AA response received in a PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REJECT message?
results.reference: The UE passes the service-level-AA response to the upper layer.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.1A, Service-level authentication and authorization procedure
results.model_answer:
Based on Clause 6.3.1A ([1]/[2]), when the UE receives the service-level-AA response in the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REJECT message, the UE **passes it to the upper layer**.

This occurs in the context where the service-level authentication and authorization procedure was performed during the UE-requested PDU session establishment procedure and completed unsuccessfully — the SMF transports the service-level-AA response (containing the failure result) to the UE via the Service-level-AA container IE of the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REJECT message, and the UE's role is simply to forward that payload up to the upper layers, since the underlying service-level-AA exchange is transparent to the 5GSM layer itself.
results.evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.1A, Service-level authentication and authorization procedure

results.question: What two successful actions by the external DN trigger the inclusion of the EAP message information element?
results.reference: The successful authentication and successful authorization of the UE performed by the external DN using EAP trigger the inclusion of this IE.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.3.2.8, EAP message
results.model_answer:
Based on Clause 8.3.2.8 (and its counterpart [6]), the EAP message IE is included when the external DN successfully performs **authentication** and **authorization** of the UE using EAP.

So the two successful actions are:
1. **Authentication** of the UE by the external DN (via EAP)
2. **Authorization** of the UE by the external DN (via EAP)

results.question: How does the external DN's use of EAP relate to the presence of the EAP message information element?
results.reference: The EAP message IE is present specifically as a result of the external DN utilizing the EAP protocol to successfully authenticate and authorize the UE.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.3.2.8, EAP message
results.model_answer:
Based on the context provided, the presence of the EAP message IE is directly conditioned on whether the external DN used EAP for authentication and authorization of the UE, and on the **outcome** of that EAP-based authentication/authorization:

**In the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT ACCEPT message (Clause 8.3.2.8 - EAP message):**
- The EAP message IE is included **when the external DN successfully performed** authentication and authorization of the UE using EAP.
- This carries the **EAP-success** message, consistent with [7]/[8], which states that when DN authentication completes successfully during the UE-requested PDU session establishment procedure, the EAP-success message is transported in the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT ACCEPT message.

**In the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REJECT message (Clause 8.3.3.4 - EAP message):**
- The EAP message IE is included **when the external DN unsuccessfully performed** authentication and authorization of the UE using EAP.
- This carries the **EAP-failure** message, consistent with [7]/[8], which states that when DN authentication completes unsuccessfully, the EAP-failure message is transported in the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REJECT message.

**Relationship summary:**
The EAP message IE's inclusion is a **conditional/optional** field whose presence signals that the external DN actually engaged EAP-based authentication and authorization for the UE (as opposed to no authentication being performed, or authentication being performed by other means). Its presence and content (success vs. failure) directly reflect:
1. **That EAP was used** by the external DN as the authentication/authorization mechanism (per Clause 6.3.1.1 [7]/[8], EAP is the protocol used by the network to authenticate the UE's upper layers when DN-based PDU session authentication and authorization is required).
2. **The outcome** of that EAP exchange — success maps to the IE appearing in the ACCEPT message (carrying EAP-success), while failure maps to the IE appearing in the REJECT message (carrying EAP-failure).

Thus, the EAP message IE serves as the **transport container** for the terminal EAP message (EAP-success or EAP-failure) generated as a result of the external DN's EAP-based authentication/authorization process, and its presence in either the ACCEPT or REJECT message is contingent on whether that external DN authentication/authorization using EAP was actually performed and what its result was. If the external DN does not use EAP at all (e.g., PDU session authentication/authorization is not required or not performed), this IE would not be included in either message.

results.question: What role does the external DN play in the scenario that leads to the EAP message IE being included?
results.reference: The external DN plays the active role of performing and successfully completing UE authentication and authorization using EAP, which is the prerequisite for including the IE.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.3.2.8, EAP message
results.model_answer:
The external DN acts as the authenticator in EAP-based secondary authentication/authorization of the PDU session: it performs (attempts) the authentication and authorization of the UE via EAP, and the outcome of that DN-side EAP processing determines whether the EAP message IE carries a success or failure result.

- If the external DN **successfully** authenticates/authorizes the UE via EAP, the EAP message IE (as sent in the ESTABLISHMENT ACCEPT, per [3]/[4]) is included to convey that successful EAP outcome to the UE.
- If the external DN **unsuccessfully** authenticates/authorizes the UE via EAP, the EAP message IE (as sent in the ESTABLISHMENT REJECT, per [5]/[6]) is included to convey that failure, together with 5GSM cause #29 "user authentication or authorization failed" as described in the abnormal-case handling ([1]/[2]).

So the external DN is the entity actually performing the EAP authentication/authorization decision (success or failure) for the PDU session, and the SMF relays that DN-generated EAP result to the UE via the EAP message IE — the IE's presence and content are entirely driven by whether the external DN accepted or rejected the UE's authentication/authorization via EAP.

results.question: How does the NAS protocol handle uplink user data packets in a PDU session with IPv4v6 PDU session type?
results.reference: The NAS protocol enables different forwarding treatments of UL user data packets in one or more QoS flows based on signalled QoS rules, derived QoS rules, or any combination of them.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.2.5.1.1.1, General
results.model_answer:
Based on clause 6.2.5.1.1.1, for a PDU session of **IPv4v6 PDU session type**, the NAS protocol enables **different forwarding treatments of uplink (UL) user data packets across one or more QoS flows**. This differentiation is based on:

- **Signalled QoS rules**, or
- **Derived QoS rules**, or
- **Any combination of them**

This means that UL user data packets within an IPv4v6 PDU session are **not necessarily treated uniformly**; instead, they can be classified and mapped to different QoS flows depending on the applicable QoS rules (whether provided by the network or derived by the UE), allowing differentiated forwarding treatment per packet/flow.

This is explicitly contrasted with the **Unstructured PDU session type**, where all UL user data packets are associated with the **same single QoS flow**, with no such differentiation.

results.question: Why are all uplink user data packets associated with the same QoS flow in an Unstructured PDU session type?
results.reference: In a PDU session of Unstructured PDU session type, all UL user data packets are associated with the same QoS flow as specified by the protocol.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.2.5.1.1.1, General
results.model_answer:
Because in an **Unstructured PDU session**, the user-plane payload has no IP (or Ethernet) header structure that the UE/network can inspect to classify traffic against packet filters. QoS rules (signalled or derived) rely on packet filters built from IP/Ethernet header fields (addresses, ports, protocol, etc.) to differentiate UL traffic and map it to different QoS flows.

Since Unstructured PDU session type carries opaque/non-IP data with no such header fields available for filtering:

- No packet filters can be constructed or matched against the data.
- Consequently, no QoS rule other than the default QoS rule can be created — this is explicitly reflected in the error-handling logic in [3]/[4]: e.g., "When the rule operation is 'Create new QoS rule', the DQR bit is set to 'the QoS rule is not the default QoS rule', and the PDU session type of the PDU session is 'Unstructured'" is treated as a semantic error, and a non-empty packet filter list in the default QoS rule for an Unstructured PDU session is also flagged as a syntactical error.
- Similarly, derived (reflective) QoS rules are stated in [7] to be "applicable only for PDU session of IPv4, IPv6, IPv4v6 or Ethernet PDU session type" — explicitly excluding Unstructured type, since reflective QoS also depends on inspecting IP packet headers.

With no basis (no packet filters, no derived rules) to differentiate traffic, the NAS protocol cannot enable "different forwarding treatments" for UL data in an Unstructured PDU session. Therefore, by design, only the default QoS rule (and its single associated QoS flow, identified by the QFI of the default QoS rule) applies, and all UL user data packets are forced onto that same QoS flow, as stated in [1]/[2].

results.question: What mechanism allows for differentiated forwarding of uplink packets in an Ethernet PDU session?
results.reference: The NAS protocol enables different forwarding treatments based on signalled QoS rules, derived QoS rules, or any combination of them for UL user data packets in one or more QoS flows.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.2.5.1.1.1, General
results.model_answer:
In an Ethernet PDU session type, differentiated forwarding treatment of UL user data packets across one or more QoS flows is achieved through **QoS rules** — specifically:

- **Signalled QoS rules** — explicitly provided by the network, and/or
- **Derived QoS rules** — created by the UE itself via **reflective QoS**, based on DL user data packets received on the PDU session

Since Ethernet is one of the PDU session types (along with IPv4, IPv6, IPv4v6) for which derived QoS rules are applicable, the UE can generate these derived rules by inspecting downlink Ethernet packets and reflecting their characteristics (e.g., associated QFI) to create matching UL packet filters. Each derived QoS rule contains a QFI, a UL packet filter, and a precedence value of 80 (decimal), and is governed by timer T3583.

Thus, the combination of signalled QoS rules and/or reflective-QoS-derived rules — mapping UL Ethernet packets to specific QoS flows via packet filters — is the mechanism that enables differentiated UL forwarding treatment in an Ethernet PDU session (as opposed to Unstructured PDU sessions, where all UL packets are forced onto a single QoS flow with no such differentiation).

results.question: How does the treatment of uplink user data packets differ between an IPv6 PDU session and an Unstructured PDU session?
results.reference: In an IPv6 PDU session, the NAS protocol enables different forwarding treatments across multiple QoS flows using QoS rules, whereas in an Unstructured PDU session, all UL packets are associated with the same QoS flow.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.2.5.1.1.1, General
results.model_answer:
Based on the context (Clause 6.2.5.1.1.1), the key difference lies in how uplink user data packets are mapped to QoS flows:

**IPv6 PDU session:**
UL user data packets can receive **different forwarding treatments across one or more QoS flows**. The NAS protocol enables this differentiation based on:
- Signalled QoS rules,
- Derived QoS rules, or
- Any combination of both.

This means an IPv6 PDU session can have multiple QoS flows, with different UL packets being routed to different flows depending on packet filtering/matching against the QoS rules (signalled and/or derived).

**Unstructured PDU session:**
All UL user data packets are associated with the **same single QoS flow**. There is no differentiation of forwarding treatment — regardless of QoS rules — because the Unstructured PDU session type does not support packet filtering into multiple flows; it is treated as a single opaque data stream mapped entirely onto one QoS flow.

**Summary of the difference:**

| Aspect | IPv6 PDU session | Unstructured PDU session |
|---|---|---|
| Number of QoS flows for UL data | One or more | Always one |
| Basis for flow assignment | Signalled QoS rules, derived QoS rules, or combination | Not applicable (single flow only) |
| Packet-level differentiation | Yes — packets can be treated differently based on QoS rule matching | No — all packets treated uniformly |

This reflects the fact that IPv6 (like IPv4, IPv4v6, and Ethernet) PDU sessions support packet filtering and QoS rule-based traffic separation, whereas Unstructured PDU sessions (carrying opaque/non-IP data) do not support such per-packet differentiation and therefore rely on a single, undifferentiated QoS flow for all uplink data.

results.question: How does a voice-centric UE in 5GMM-REGISTERED state determine when to initiate the establishment of a PDU session for IMS signalling?
results.reference: The UE receives a request from upper layers to establish the PDU session for IMS signalling when IMS voice is available over either 3GPP or non-3GPP access and the conditions for performing an initial registration with IMS specified in 3GPP TS 24.229 subclause U.3.1.2 are satisfied.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.4.1.2, UE-requested PDU session establishment procedure initiation
results.model_answer:
Based on the provided context, **there is no explicit provision** describing a voice-centric UE in 5GMM-REGISTERED state autonomously determining when to initiate establishment of a PDU session for IMS signalling based on its usage setting alone.

What the context *does* show is that PDU session establishment for IMS is triggered by other mechanisms, not directly by the "voice-centric" usage setting:

1. **Upper-layer triggered start/stop indications** [7], [8]: The 5GMM layer is informed by upper layers when services such as MMTEL voice, MMTEL video, SMSoIP, or MO IMS registration-related signalling *start*. It is this upper-layer request (e.g., to establish a PDU session with request type "initial emergency request"/"existing emergency PDU session", or an indication that an MMTEL/SMSoIP/IMS registration service is starting) that causes the UE to initiate the establishment of a PDU session for IMS (DNN = "IMS"), not a determination made purely from the "voice-centric" setting.

2. **Fallback to E-UTRA/EPC upon barring** [7], [8]: If the UE is voice-centric and operating in single-registration mode, and access barring applies (all categories except 0 and 2, or except 0) while an MMTEL voice/video call is ongoing, the UE **may** attempt to select an E-UTRA cell connected to EPC and then proceed with EMM/ESM procedures (per subclause 4.8.2 and TS 24.301) "to make a PDN connection providing access to IMS available." Similarly, if SMSoIP or MO IMS registration signalling is ongoing and barred in NR/5GC, the UE may fall back to E-UTRA/EPC to obtain the PDN connection for IMS.

3. **IMS voice availability determination** [1], [2], [4], [6]: The voice-centric setting mainly governs whether the UE disables its N1 mode capability (for 3GPP or non-3GPP access) when "IMS voice not available" is determined — this affects *access selection* (e.g., falling back to E-UTRA/EPC for voice domain selection per TS 24.301), rather than directly triggering IMS PDU session establishment.

**Conclusion**: Within the given context, the decision to *initiate* establishment of a PDU session for IMS signalling is driven by explicit upper-layer service-start indications (e.g., for MMTEL, SMSoIP, MO IMS registration) or by fallback procedures triggered when access barring prevents use of the current RAT/CN combination — not by an independent NAS-level rule tied solely to the UE being voice-centric and 5GMM-REGISTERED. The material provided does not contain a definitive standalone rule for this specific trigger, so any further detail would require content beyond what is given here.

results.question: What specific rule must a TWIF acting on behalf of an N5CW device follow when allocating a PDU session ID for a new PDU session establishment request?
results.reference: The TWIF acting on behalf of the N5CW device must allocate the 'PDU session identity value 15' for the new PDU session.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.4.1.2, UE-requested PDU session establishment procedure initiation
results.model_answer:
When the TWIF, acting on behalf of the N5CW device, requests to establish a new PDU session, it **shall allocate "PDU session identity value 15"** for that PDU session ID (as specified in subclause 6.4.1.2 / clause 4.7.5).

This differs from the rule for an N5CW device that itself supports 3GPP access: in that case, the device requesting a new PDU session via 3GPP access must **refrain from** allocating "PDU session identity value 15" (to avoid conflicting with the value reserved for TWIF-initiated sessions). The TWIF, however, is specifically required to use value 15 when it establishes the PDU session on the device's behalf.

results.question: Under what three conditions must the SMF initiate the UUAA-SM procedure instead of immediately accepting or rejecting a PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST message containing a Service-level-AA container?
results.reference: The SMF must initiate the UUAA-SM procedure when: a) service-level authentication and authorization by the external DN is required due to local policy, b) there is valid user subscription information for the requested DNN (or DNN and S-NSSAI), and c) the Service-level-AA container includes CAA-level UAV ID.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.4.1.2, UE-requested PDU session establishment procedure initiation
results.model_answer:
## Three Conditions Triggering SMF-Initiated UUAA-SM

Based on the interplay between clause 4.22.2 (UUAA authentication and authorization of UAV) and clause 6.4.1.4.1 (PDU session establishment reject causes), the SMF shall initiate the UUAA-SM procedure — rather than immediately accepting the PDU session establishment or rejecting it outright — only when **all three** of the following conditions are simultaneously met:

**1. The UE has supplied a valid CAA-level UAV ID in the Service-level-AA container IE**
The PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST message must include the Service-level-AA container IE with the service-level device ID set to the CAA-level UAV ID. If this ID is *absent* and subscription data requires UUAA-SM, the SMF does not trigger UUAA-SM at all — it immediately rejects the request with 5GSM cause #86 "UAS services not allowed" (per clause 6.4.1.4.1). Thus, presence of the UAV ID is a precondition for the SMF to even attempt UUAA-SM rather than reject outright.

**2. The SM subscription data (and/or operator policy) indicates that UUAA-SM is required for this UE/PDU session**
Per clause 4.22.2, the SMF's decision to trigger UUAA-SM is conditioned on the SM subscription data requiring it. If UUAA-SM is not required by subscription/policy, the SMF has no basis to initiate the procedure and would proceed to accept/reject the PDU session establishment through ordinary SM processing, without invoking service-level-AA signalling.

**3. The PDU session being established is a non-emergency PDU session**
Per clause 6.3.1A, the service-level authentication and authorization procedure (which UUAA-SM uses) "can be performed only during or after the UE-requested PDU session procedure establishing a non-emergency PDU session" and "shall not be performed during or after the UE-requested PDU session establishment procedure establishing an emergency PDU session." Hence, even if conditions 1 and 2 are satisfied, if the request type is for an emergency PDU session, the SMF must not invoke UUAA-SM and must handle the request through the normal (non-UUAA) establishment/reject logic.

**Summary:** Only when (i) the UE includes the CAA-level UAV ID in the Service-level-AA container, (ii) subscription data/operator policy mandates UUAA-SM for that UE, and (iii) the requested PDU session is non-emergency, does the SMF defer its accept/reject decision and instead initiate the UUAA-SM exchange (SERVICE-LEVEL AUTHENTICATION COMMAND/COMPLETE signalling) before finally including the service-level-AA response in the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT ACCEPT or REJECT message.
results.evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.1A, Service-level authentication and authorization procedure

results.question: How does the UE's NAS perspective generally treat procedures and messages for 5GMM and 5GSM when comparing non-3GPP access to 3GPP access?
results.reference: From the UE's NAS perspective, the procedures and messages defined for 5GMM and 5GSM are generally used in the same way over non-3GPP access as they are over 3GPP access.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.7.1, General
results.model_answer: From the UE's NAS perspective, the 5GMM and 5GSM procedures and messages are, in general, used the same way over non-3GPP access as over 3GPP access — i.e., the same procedures/messages defined for 3GPP access are reused for non-3GPP access. However, this is not an absolute equivalence: a number of specific aspects differ between the two accesses, and these differences are detailed in the subsequent subclauses (e.g., clause 4.7.2 for 5GMM aspects and clause 4.7.3 for 5GSM aspects), such as independent 5GMM state machines per access, non-applicability of certain features (MICO, DRX, paging, CIoT optimizations, LADN, etc.) for non-3GPP access, and differences in registration, establishment cause determination, and session management rate control mechanisms.

results.question: Why might a UE's NAS experience differences when operating over non-3GPP access despite the general rule for 5GMM and 5GSM procedures?
results.reference: Although the general rule is that procedures and messages are used the same way, a number of specific aspects are different for non-3GPP access, as detailed in subsequent subclauses.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.7.1, General
results.model_answer:
Because clause 4.7.1's general rule that 5GMM/5GSM procedures and messages are used the same way over non-3GPP access as over 3GPP access is explicitly qualified — the clause itself states that "a number of aspects are different," which are then detailed in the following subclauses (4.7.2 for mobility management aspects and 4.7.3 for session management aspects).

Concretely, these differences include:

- **Establishment cause selection (4.7.2.2):** Over non-3GPP access, the UE must go through an additional determination process — identifying applicable access identities and then mapping the access attempt (e.g., emergency session, MO signalling, MO data, MMTel voice/video call, SMSoIP) to a specific establishment cause using the rules in Table 4.7.2.2.1. This is a non-3GPP-access-specific procedure not mirrored identically for 3GPP access.

- **Session management exceptions (4.7.3):** Several 5GSM features that apply over 3GPP access do **not** apply over non-3GPP access, namely:
  a) Serving PLMN rate control
  b) Small data rate control
  c) Handling of 5GSM cause #82 (maximum data rate per UE for user-plane integrity protection too low)
  d) MBS (Multicast/Broadcast Services)
  e) Support of redundant PDU sessions

- **Connection management procedure limitations (5.1.2):** Certain network-initiated 5GMM connection management procedures (e.g., paging/N1 connection establishment requests) are explicitly stated as "not applicable for the non-3GPP access network," meaning the network cannot use the same triggering mechanisms over non-3GPP access as it does over 3GPP access.

- **SNPN-related interactions (4.14.2):** When accessing SNPN services via a PLMN, or PLMN services via an SNPN, the access is always treated as **untrusted non-3GPP access** from the UE's NAS perspective, even though the underlying access might conceptually be 3GPP-based. This introduces non-3GPP-specific NAS handling (parameters, procedures) as a structural consequence of how SNPN/PLMN interworking is defined.

Thus, while the overarching architecture keeps 5GMM/5GSM procedures conceptually unified across access types, the specification carves out specific behavioral differences — in establishment cause determination, session management feature applicability, and certain procedure applicability — because the underlying non-3GPP access transport, paging capability, and certain rate-control/service assumptions do not hold in the same way as they do over 3GPP access.

results.question: How does the clause qualify its general statement about NAS procedures over non-3GPP access?
results.reference: It qualifies the general statement by noting that there are a number of aspects which are different, and these differences are described in the following subclauses.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.7.1, General
results.model_answer:
Based on Clause 4.7.1 (General), the clause makes a broad opening statement that, from the UE's NAS perspective, the procedures and messages defined for 5GMM and 5GSM are generally used over non-3GPP access **in the same way as** over 3GPP access.

However, it immediately qualifies this general statement by noting that **"a number of aspects are different"**, and it defers the details of these differences to the following subclauses:

- **Subclause 4.7.2** – 5GS mobility management aspects (which lists specific exceptions such as independent 5GMM state machines per access, no dual-registration mode over non-3GPP, different RPLMNs possible, no list-based registration area management, no periodic registration updates, UE-initiated service request specifics, no paging, no LADN, no MICO, no CIoT optimizations, no unified access control, no RACS, no CAG, etc.)
- **Subclause 4.7.3** – 5GS session management aspects (which lists exceptions such as no serving PLMN rate control, no small data rate control, no handling of 5GSM cause #82, no MBS, and no support of redundant PDU sessions over non-3GPP access)

Thus, the clause's qualification is structured as a **"reuse-with-exceptions"** approach: it asserts general applicability of 3GPP-access NAS procedures to non-3GPP access, but explicitly flags that this is not absolute — the applicability is **conditional on the exceptions enumerated in the referenced subclauses (4.7.2 and 4.7.3)**, which override or modify the general rule for specific mobility and session management behaviors.

results.question: How does the 5GMM sublayer interact with upper layers when receiving a request to establish a NAS signalling connection?
results.reference: The 5GMM sublayer forwards the request to the lower layers to establish the RRC connection, as it acts as an intermediary between upper layers and lower layers for NAS signalling connection establishment.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.2.9, Interaction with upper layers
results.model_answer:
Based on the provided context (clauses 4.5.4.2/[1][2] and 4.5.5/[7][8]), the relevant interactions with upper layers that are specified concern **access attempts** categorized by NAS for the purpose of access barring, rather than a generic "request to establish a NAS signalling connection" as such. There is no clause in the given context that describes upper layers directly requesting establishment of the N1 NAS signalling connection itself; instead, upper-layer requests trigger specific *events* (e.g., MMTEL voice/video call start, SMS over NAS, PDU session establishment/modification, LCS, UE policy signalling, etc.), and 5GMM's interaction with upper layers is driven by the **outcome of access control checking** for the corresponding access attempt:

**1. Categorization and submission to lower layers**
When such an event occurs while the UE is in 5GMM-CONNECTED mode (or CONNECTED with RRC inactive indication), NAS categorizes the attempt into access identities and an access category (per subclause 4.5.2/4.5.2A and 4.5.3) and passes these, together with an optional RRC establishment cause, to the lower layers for access control checking.

**2. If lower layers indicate the attempt is allowed**
- For service-indication type events (MMTEL voice/video call start, SMSoIP start, MO IMS registration-related signalling start), NAS **notifies the upper layers that the access attempt is allowed**.
- For other request-driven events (SMS over NAS, PDU session establishment/modification, user-plane re-establishment, LCS request, UE policy container transport), NAS does **not** send an explicit "allowed" notification to upper layers; instead it proceeds directly to invoke the appropriate procedure (NAS transport, service request, etc.) to fulfil the request.

**3. If lower layers indicate the attempt is barred**
- For the service-indication events, NAS **notifies the upper layers that the access attempt is barred**, and subsequently, once the lower layers indicate that barring is alleviated for the associated access category, NAS **notifies the upper layers that the barring is alleviated**.
- For the other request-driven events (SMS, PDU session establishment/modification, service request for user-plane re-establishment, LCS, UE policy container), NAS does not immediately notify upper layers of barring via an explicit primitive; rather, it simply refrains from initiating the corresponding NAS procedure, and may initiate it later (if still needed) upon an indication from lower layers that barring is alleviated.

**4. Exception/double-barring avoidance (clause 4.5.5)**
For service request or registration procedures triggered for NAS signalling connection recovery, or following a fallback indication from lower layers, access control checking is skipped entirely to avoid double barring — the access category is still determined (for deriving the RRC establishment cause), and the NAS proceeds directly to send the initial NAS message, without requiring a fresh "allowed" indication from lower layers or notification to upper layers.

**Summary:** The 5GMM sublayer does not have a direct upper-layer request "to establish a NAS signalling connection" as an isolated action in this context; rather, upper-layer requests (for services, SMS, PDU session procedures, LCS, policy signalling) trigger NAS to determine access category/identities, submit them for access barring checks, and then either invoke the relevant NAS procedure (if allowed) or withhold it while informing upper layers of the barring status only for the IMS/MMTEL/SMSoIP/IMS-registration type indications — with barring-alleviation notifications following the same pattern once received from the lower layers.

results.question: Under what specific condition is the Allowed SSC mode IE included in a network response?
results.reference: The IE is included when the network rejects a PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST with the specific cause '#68 "not supported SSC mode"'.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.3.3.3, Allowed SSC mode
results.model_answer:
The **Allowed SSC mode IE** is included in a **PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REJECT message** specifically when the network rejects the PDU session establishment with **5GSM cause value #68 "not supported SSC mode"**.

This occurs when:
- The PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST message contains an **SSC mode IE indicating an SSC mode that is not supported** by the subscription, the SMF configuration, or both; and
- The SMF **decides to reject** the PDU session establishment request based on this unsupported SSC mode.

In this case, per Clause 8.3.3.3, the SMF shall include:
- The **5GSM cause value #68** "not supported SSC mode" in the 5GSM cause IE, **and**
- The **SSC modes allowed by the SMF** in the **Allowed SSC mode IE** of the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REJECT message.

This allows the network to inform the UE which SSC modes are acceptable, so the UE can potentially re-attempt the PDU session establishment procedure using one of the allowed SSC modes.

results.question: How does the network use the Allowed SSC mode IE when rejecting a session establishment?
results.reference: The network includes the IE to convey information about allowed SSC modes when rejecting the request due to an unsupported SSC mode.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.3.3.3, Allowed SSC mode
results.model_answer:
The **Allowed SSC mode IE** is included in the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REJECT message specifically in conjunction with **5GSM cause value #68 "not supported SSC mode"**.

Specifically:

- If the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST message contains an SSC mode IE indicating an SSC mode that is **not supported** by the subscription, the SMF configuration, or both, and the SMF decides to reject the PDU session establishment, the SMF shall:
  - Include **5GSM cause value #68 "not supported SSC mode"** in the 5GSM cause IE, **and**
  - Include the **SSC modes allowed by the SMF** in the **Allowed SSC mode IE** of the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REJECT message.

This IE is only included when the rejection cause is #68 (as confirmed by clause 8.3.3.3: "This IE is included when the network rejects the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST with cause #68 'not supported SSC mode'").
