**Purpose/effect on the UE:** By providing the Allowed SSC mode IE, the network informs the UE which SSC mode(s) it can use instead. This directly influences UE behavior for future attempts:

- Upon receiving cause #68, the UE shall ignore the Back-off timer value IE and Re-attempt indicator IE (if any).
- The UE evaluates URSP rules (if available).
- The UE shall **not** send another PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST for the same DNN (or no DNN) and the same (mapped) HPLMN S-NSSAI (or no S-NSSAI) using:
  - the same (rejected) SSC mode, or
  - any SSC mode **not included** in the Allowed SSC mode IE

  until one of the following occurs:
  - the UE registers to a new PLMN not in the equivalent PLMN list (at time of rejection)
  - the UE changes the SSC mode it uses for that DNN/S-NSSAI, requesting a new SSC mode from the Allowed SSC mode IE or no SSC mode
  - the UE is switched off
  - the USIM is removed / SNPN subscriber list entry is updated

Thus, the Allowed SSC mode IE effectively constrains and guides subsequent UE PDU session establishment attempts by explicitly indicating the SSC mode(s) the network will accept, preventing repeated rejected attempts with unsupported SSC modes.

results.question: What triggers the inclusion of the Allowed SSC mode IE according to the clause?
results.reference: The trigger is the network's decision to reject a PDU session establishment request with cause value #68, indicating the requested SSC mode is not supported.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.3.3.3, Allowed SSC mode
results.model_answer: The **Allowed SSC mode IE** is included when the network **rejects the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST** message with **5GSM cause #68 "not supported SSC mode"**.
results.evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.6.2.3, Provision of NSSAI to lower layers in 5GMM-IDLE mode

results.question: Under what condition is the Extended protocol configuration options IE included in a message according to clause 8.3.2.10?
results.reference: It is included when the network needs to transmit protocol data to the UE.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.3.2.10, Extended protocol configuration options
results.model_answer: According to clause 8.3.2.10, the Extended protocol configuration options IE is included in the message **when the network needs to transmit (protocol) data (e.g., configuration parameters, error codes, or messages/events) to the UE**.
results.evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.3.2.10, Extended protocol configuration options

results.question: What is the purpose of the Extended protocol configuration options IE as defined in clause 8.3.2.10?
results.reference: Its purpose is to allow the network to send protocol data, such as configuration parameters, error codes, or messages/events, to the UE.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.3.2.10, Extended protocol configuration options
results.model_answer:
Per Clause 8.3.2.10, the Extended protocol configuration options IE is included in the message **when the network needs to transmit (protocol) data (e.g., configuration parameters, error codes or messages/events) to the UE**.

This describes the network-to-UE direction of use for this IE, as defined in that specific clause context.
results.evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.3.2.10, Extended protocol configuration options

results.question: In what specific case is the network prohibited from using the NOTIFICATION message to re-establish user-plane resources for PDU sessions associated with non-3GPP access over 3GPP access?
results.reference: The network is prohibited if all the PDU sessions of the UE that are established over the 3GPP access are associated with control plane only indication.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.6.3.1, General
results.model_answer: The network shall not use the NOTIFICATION message to re-establish user-plane resources of PDU session(s) associated with non-3GPP access over 3GPP access **if all the PDU sessions of the UE that are established over the 3GPP access are associated with control plane only indication**.

results.question: What three conditions must all be true for the network to be prohibited from using the NOTIFICATION message over non-3GPP access?
results.reference: The three conditions are: a) the MUSIM UE supports the paging indication for voice services, b) the network has indicated 'paging indication for voice services supported' to the UE, and c) the AMF detects that the downlink data is related to voice service.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.6.3.1, General
results.model_answer:
Based on clauses [6]/[7], the network shall **not** use the NOTIFICATION message over non-3GPP access when **all three** of the following conditions are true simultaneously:

a) **The MUSIM UE supports the paging indication for voice services**

b) **The network has indicated "paging indication for voice services supported" to the UE**

c) **The AMF detects that the downlink data is related to voice service** (see 3GPP TS 23.501 [8])

Only when all three conditions hold together is the network prohibited from sending the NOTIFICATION message over non-3GPP access — presumably because, in this case, the paging restriction mechanism for voice services is expected to be used instead to avoid disrupting an ongoing or higher-priority voice-related connection (e.g., on another USIM in a MUSIM UE).

results.question: Under what conditions must the SMF set the Authorized QoS rules IE in the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND message when initiating a network-requested PDU session modification?
results.reference: The SMF must set the Authorized QoS rules IE when the authorized QoS rules of the PDU session are modified or are marked as to be synchronized with the UE.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.2.2, Network-requested PDU session modification procedure initiation
results.model_answer:
The SMF **shall** set the Authorized QoS rules IE in the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND message only when either (or both) of the following conditions hold for the PDU session:

1. **The authorized QoS rules of the PDU session have been modified** — i.e., there is an actual change to the QoS rules (e.g., due to new/modified/deleted QoS rules or packet filters, traffic segregation handling, etc.), or

2. **The authorized QoS rules are marked as "to be synchronised" with the UE** — this typically occurs as a result of prior abnormal-case handling (e.g., after a T3591 expiry where the SMF chose to continue using the previous configuration and marked the QoS rules for resynchronization, per clause 6.3.2.5).

In either case, when setting this IE, the SMF must also ensure that the total number of packet filters used across the authorized QoS rules for the PDU session does not exceed the maximum number of packet filters supported by the UE for that PDU session (as determined either from the UE-provided "Maximum number of supported packet filters" IE during inter-system change scenarios, or the default assumption of 16 packet filters if not provided).

If neither condition (modification nor synchronization marking) applies, the SMF does not need to include the Authorized QoS rules IE in the message.
results.evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.2.2, Network-requested PDU session modification procedure initiation

results.question: How must the SMF handle service data flows for which the UE has requested traffic segregation if they have different QoS handling?
results.reference: The SMF must bind all these service data flows to a single QoS flow.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.2.2, Network-requested PDU session modification procedure initiation
results.model_answer:
According to the network-requested PDU session modification procedure initiation clause (6.3.2.2), if the UE has requested traffic segregation for **multiple service data flows with different QoS handling**, the SMF shall **bind all these service data flows to a single QoS flow**.

This is part of the broader rule that the SMF shall use **only one dedicated QoS flow for traffic segregation** — meaning even when the service data flows differ in QoS handling, the SMF cannot split them across multiple dedicated QoS flows for segregation purposes; they must all be bound to that same single dedicated QoS flow. When the SMF allows this traffic segregation, it must also create a new authorized QoS rule for these service data flows and delete the corresponding packet filters from any other authorized QoS rules where they previously existed.

results.question: What must the SMF ensure regarding packet filters when setting the Authorized QoS rules IE for a PDU session?
results.reference: The SMF must ensure that the number of packet filters used in the authorized QoS rules does not exceed the maximum number of packet filters supported by the UE for that PDU session.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.2.2, Network-requested PDU session modification procedure initiation
results.model_answer:
The SMF must ensure that the number of packet filters used in the authorized QoS rules of the PDU session **does not exceed the maximum number of packet filters supported by the UE** for that PDU session.

This requirement applies consistently across the relevant procedures:

- **PDU Session Establishment** (Clause 6.4.1.3 / [3],[4]): When setting the Authorized QoS rules IE in the PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT ACCEPT message, the SMF shall ensure the number of packet filters does not exceed the maximum supported by the UE.

- **Network-requested PDU Session Modification** (Clause 6.3.2.2 / [7],[8]): When setting the Authorized QoS rules IE in the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND message, the SMF shall likewise ensure the number of packet filters used does not exceed the maximum number supported by the UE for the PDU session.

The maximum number is determined as follows:
- If the UE included a **Maximum number of supported packet filters IE** in its request message (PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT REQUEST or, for inter-system change cases, PDU SESSION MODIFICATION REQUEST), the SMF uses that UE-indicated value as the limit.
- Otherwise, the SMF assumes the UE supports **16 packet filters** for the PDU session (the default value per [3]/[4]/[7]/[8]).

This constraint exists to prevent overwhelming the UE's storage/processing capability for packet filters, and ties into the UE-side error handling logic: if the UE later determines that the number of authorized QoS rules or associated packet filters has reached its maximum supported number, the UE may reject the request (e.g., with 5GSM cause **#26 "insufficient resources"**) or, upon establishment, may initiate a PDU session release with the same cause (per [1]/[2] and [3]/[4]).

results.question: When the network-requested PDU session modification is triggered for P-CSCF restoration, and the UE had previously requested P-CSCF addresses which were provided, what must the SMF include in the Extended protocol configuration options IE?
results.reference: The SMF must include the P-CSCF IP address(es) in the Extended protocol configuration options IE of the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND message.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.2.2, Network-requested PDU session modification procedure initiation
results.model_answer:
The SMF shall include the **P‑CSCF IP address(es)** in the Extended protocol configuration options IE of the PDU SESSION MODIFICATION COMMAND message, formatted as specified in subclause 5.8.2.2 of 3GPP TS 23.380 [54].

This applies specifically when:
- The UE had earlier requested a P‑CSCF IPv6 address or P‑CSCF IPv4 address, **and**
- The SMF had already provided the P‑CSCF address(es) during the original PDU session establishment procedure, **and**
- The network-requested PDU session modification procedure is now triggered for the purpose of **P‑CSCF restoration**.

results.question: What are the two distinct scenarios in which the AMF sets the PRTI IE in a RELAY KEY REJECT message, and what determines which value is used?
results.reference: The AMF sets the PRTI IE to either the PRTI value from the received RELAY KEY REQUEST message if the network decides to reject that request, or to the PRTI value from the received RELAY AUTHENTICATION RESPONSE message if the AMF receives an EAP-failure message from the AUSF.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.5.4.5, UE-initiated authentication and key agreement procedure not accepted by the network
results.model_answer:
Based on Clause 5.5.4.5, the AMF sets the PRTI IE in the RELAY KEY REJECT message according to **two distinct rejection scenarios**, determined by **the point in the procedure at which the network decides to reject**:

## Scenario 1: Rejection at the Initial Request Stage

**Condition:** The network decides to reject the **RELAY KEY REQUEST message** itself (i.e., the rejection occurs before any authentication exchange has taken place).

**PRTI Value Used:** The AMF sets the PRTI IE to the **PRTI value of the received RELAY KEY REQUEST message**.

This applies when the AMF/network rejects the UE-initiated procedure outright, without proceeding into the EAP-AKA' authentication exchange with the AUSF.

## Scenario 2: Rejection Following EAP-Failure During Authentication

**Condition:** The AMF has already progressed into the authentication exchange (i.e., RELAY AUTHENTICATION REQUEST/RESPONSE messages have been exchanged), and the AMF **receives an EAP-failure message from the AUSF**.

**PRTI Value Used:** The AMF sets the PRTI IE to the **PRTI value of the received RELAY AUTHENTICATION RESPONSE message**, and additionally includes the **EAP message IE** set with the **EAP-failure message**.

---

### Summary of the Determining Factor

| Scenario | Trigger | PRTI Source | Additional IE |
|----------|---------|--------------|----------------|
| 1 | Network rejects the RELAY KEY REQUEST outright | PRTI from RELAY KEY REQUEST | None specified |
| 2 | AUSF returns EAP-failure during authentication | PRTI from RELAY AUTHENTICATION RESPONSE | EAP message IE (EAP-failure) |

**The key determinant** is **whether the rejection occurs before or after the EAP-AKA' authentication exchange has begun**:
- If rejection happens **immediately upon receiving the RELAY KEY REQUEST** (no AUSF interaction yet, or the AMF simply declines the request), the PRTI echoes back the **original request's PRTI**.
- If rejection happens **as a result of the AUSF signaling authentication failure** (via EAP-failure) after one or more RELAY AUTHENTICATION REQUEST/RESPONSE exchanges have occurred, the PRTI reflects the **most recent RELAY AUTHENTICATION RESPONSE's PRTI**, since that exchange is the one being rejected.

results.question: How does the content of the RELAY KEY REJECT message differ when the AMF receives an EAP-failure message from the AUSF compared to when the network decides to reject the RELAY KEY REQUEST?
results.reference: When the AMF receives an EAP-failure message from the AUSF, it includes the EAP message IE set with an EAP-failure message in the RELAY KEY REJECT message. When the network decides to reject the RELAY KEY REQUEST, there is no mention of including an EAP message IE.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.5.4.5, UE-initiated authentication and key agreement procedure not accepted by the network
results.model_answer:
When the AMF rejects because the **AUSF sent an EAP-failure message**, the RELAY KEY REJECT message contains:

- **PRTI IE** set to the PRTI value of the **received RELAY AUTHENTICATION RESPONSE message**
- An **EAP message IE**, set to the EAP-failure message

When the **network itself decides to reject the RELAY KEY REQUEST** message (i.e., rejection occurs before/without AUSF involvement via EAP), the RELAY KEY REJECT message contains only:

- **PRTI IE** set to the PRTI value of the **received RELAY KEY REQUEST message**
- No EAP message IE is included

So the key differences are:
1. **Source of the PRTI value** — taken from the RELAY AUTHENTICATION RESPONSE message in the EAP-failure case, versus from the RELAY KEY REQUEST message in the network-decision case.
2. **Presence of the EAP message IE** — included (carrying the EAP-failure message) only in the case where the AUSF signaled EAP-failure; absent when the network directly rejects the RELAY KEY REQUEST.

results.question: What are the sequential actions the AMF must take when the UE-initiated authentication and key agreement procedure is not accepted?
results.reference: The AMF must 1) create a RELAY KEY REJECT message, 2) set its PRTI IE based on the specific rejection scenario, and 3) send the RELAY KEY REJECT message to the UE.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.5.4.5, UE-initiated authentication and key agreement procedure not accepted by the network
results.model_answer:
When the UE‑initiated authentication and key agreement procedure is not accepted by the network, the AMF shall, in sequence:

1. **Create a RELAY KEY REJECT message.**

2. **Set the PRTI IE of the RELAY KEY REJECT message**, depending on the reason for rejection:
   - If the network decides to reject the RELAY KEY REQUEST message → set the PRTI IE to the PRTI value of the received **RELAY KEY REQUEST** message; **or**
   - If the AMF receives an EAP‑failure message from the AUSF → set the PRTI IE to the PRTI value of the received **RELAY AUTHENTICATION RESPONSE** message, and additionally include the **EAP message IE** set to the EAP‑failure message.

3. **Send the RELAY KEY REJECT message to the UE.**

Upon receiving this RELAY KEY REJECT message, the UE considers the authentication to have failed and proceeds with the PC5 signalling protocol procedure as specified in subclause 7.2.2.5 of 3GPP TS 24.554.

results.question: What is the consequence for the UE upon receiving a RELAY KEY REJECT message, and what subsequent action must it take?
results.reference: The UE must consider the authentication has failed and must perform the PC5 signalling protocol procedure as specified in 3GPP 24.554 subclause 7.2.2.5.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.5.4.5, UE-initiated authentication and key agreement procedure not accepted by the network
results.model_answer:
Upon receiving a **RELAY KEY REJECT** message, the UE (acting as the 5G ProSe layer-3 UE-to-network relay UE) shall:

1. **Consequence:** Consider that the authentication has **failed**.

2. **Subsequent action:** Perform the PC5 signalling protocol procedure as specified in subclause 7.2.2.5 of 3GPP TS 24.554 [19E] — i.e., it must handle the failure at the PC5 layer, informing/interacting with the 5G ProSe remote UE via the PC5 signalling protocol to reflect the authentication rejection (rather than continuing with the relay key negotiation).

results.question: How does the AMF determine the value of the non-3GPP implicit de-registration timer when T3346 is greater than the non-3GPP de-registration timer in specific NAS messages?
results.reference: The AMF sets the non-3GPP implicit de-registration timer value to be 8 minutes greater than the value of timer T3346 when T3346 is greater than the non-3GPP de-registration timer and the T3346 value IE is provided in DEREGISTRATION REQUEST (with 3GPP access type), REGISTRATION REJECT during mobility/periodic registration update, or SERVICE REJECT messages.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.3.7, Handling of the periodic registration update timer and mobile reachable timer
results.model_answer: Based on the context (clause 5.3.7), when the AMF provides the T3346 value IE in a **DEREGISTRATION REQUEST message with Access type set to "3GPP access" in the Deregistration type IE**, a **REGISTRATION REJECT message during a registration procedure for mobility and periodic registration update**, or a **SERVICE REJECT message**, and the value of timer **T3346 is greater than the value of the non-3GPP de-registration timer**, the AMF sets the **non-3GPP implicit de-registration timer value to be 8 minutes greater than the value of timer T3346**.

results.question: Under what condition does the UE reset and start the non-3GPP de-registration timer, and when is this timer stopped?
results.reference: The UE registered over non-3GPP access resets and starts the non-3GPP de-registration timer when the N1 NAS signalling connection over non-3GPP access is released. The timer is stopped when certain NAS messages are received or when specific conditions are met, as indicated by the ellipsis in the clause.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.3.7, Handling of the periodic registration update timer and mobile reachable timer
results.model_answer:
Based on clause 5.3.7, the UE registered over non-3GPP access **resets and starts** the non-3GPP de-registration timer when:

- **The N1 NAS signalling connection over non-3GPP access is released.**

The timer is **stopped** when either of the following occurs:

- **The UE enters 5GMM-CONNECTED mode over non-3GPP access; or**
- **The UE enters the 5GMM-DEREGISTERED state over non-3GPP access.**

Additionally, if this timer expires before the UE contacts the network over the non-3GPP access, the UE shall enter the state 5GMM-DEREGISTERED over non-3GPP access.

results.question: How does the UE adjust the non-3GPP de-registration timer value when receiving T3346 in specific messages where T3346 exceeds the current timer value?
results.reference: The UE sets the non-3GPP de-registration timer value to be 4 minutes greater than the value of timer T3346 when it receives T3346 value IE in DEREGISTRATION REQUEST (with 3GPP access type), REGISTRATION REJECT during mobility/periodic registration update, or SERVICE REJECT messages and T3346 is greater than the current non-3GPP de-registration timer value.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.3.7, Handling of the periodic registration update timer and mobile reachable timer
results.model_answer: When the UE receives the T3346 value IE—delivered in a DEREGISTRATION REQUEST message (with Access type set to "3GPP access" in the Deregistration type IE), a REGISTRATION REJECT message during a registration procedure for mobility and periodic registration update, or a SERVICE REJECT message—and the value of timer T3346 is greater than the value of the non-3GPP de-registration timer, the UE sets the non-3GPP de-registration timer value to be **4 minutes greater than the value of timer T3346**.

results.question: What triggers the AMF to start a non-3GPP implicit de-registration timer for a UE registered over non-3GPP access?
results.reference: The AMF starts a non-3GPP implicit de-registration timer for the UE registered over non-3GPP access when the N1 NAS signalling connection over non-3GPP access is released.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.3.7, Handling of the periodic registration update timer and mobile reachable timer
results.model_answer: The AMF starts the non-3GPP implicit de-registration timer for a UE registered over non-3GPP access when the **N1 NAS signalling connection over non-3GPP access is released**.

results.question: How does the network initiate the 5G AKA based primary authentication and key agreement procedure, and what are two mandatory information elements it must include in the initiating message?
results.reference: The network initiates the procedure by sending an AUTHENTICATION REQUEST message without the EAP message IE. It must include the ngKSI and the ABBA in that message.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.1.3.1, General
results.model_answer:
The network initiates the 5G AKA based primary authentication and key agreement procedure by sending an **AUTHENTICATION REQUEST message to the UE without the EAP message IE**, and starting timer T3560. This message must include two mandatory information elements:

1. **ngKSI** – used by the UE and AMF to identify the KAMF and the partial native security context that is created if the authentication is successful.

2. **ABBA parameter** – in this release of the specification, the network shall set the length of the ABBA IE to 2, with the ABBA contents being 2 octets in length and value 0000H.

results.question: What is the purpose of the 5G AKA based primary authentication and key agreement procedure, and what keys are agreed upon as a result?
results.reference: The purpose is to provide mutual authentication between the UE and the network and to agree on the keys KAUSF, KSEAF, and KAMF.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.1.3.1, General
results.model_answer:
The purpose of the 5G AKA based primary authentication and key agreement procedure is to provide **mutual authentication between the UE and the network**, and as a result of this procedure, the UE and network agree on the following keys:

- **K_AUSF**
- **K_SEAF**
- **K_AMF**

These keys are derived after the CK and IK are computed by the USIM during a successful 5G AKA run. The ME uses CK and IK as key material to compute K_AUSF, K_SEAF, and K_AMF. Among these, K_AMF is stored in the 5G NAS security contexts of both the network and the ME (in volatile memory) while the UE is registered to the network, and serves as the root key for the 5GS integrity protection and ciphering key hierarchy.

results.question: What condition must be met for the UE to proceed with a 5G authentication challenge, and what is established in both the UE and network upon successful authentication?
results.reference: The UE shall proceed only if a USIM is present. A partial native 5G NAS security context is established in both the UE and the network when authentication is successful.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.1.3.1, General
results.model_answer:
Based on the provided text (Clause 5.4.1.3.1):

**Condition to proceed with a 5G authentication challenge:**
The UE shall proceed with a 5G authentication challenge **only if a USIM is present**.

**What is established upon successful authentication:**
A **partial native 5G NAS security context** is established in both the UE and the network when a 5G authentication is successfully performed.

During this successful 5G AKA based primary authentication and key agreement procedure:
- The **CK** and **IK** are computed by the USIM
- CK and IK are used by the ME as key material to compute new keys: **KAUSF**, **KSEAF**, and **KAMF**
- **KAMF** is stored in the 5G NAS security context of both the network and in the volatile memory of the ME while registered to the network, and serves as the root for the 5GS integrity protection and ciphering key hierarchy

Note that the generation of the new KAUSF and new KSEAF does not result in deletion of the valid (previous) KAUSF and KSEAF, if any.

Following successful completion of this procedure, the AMF shall immediately initiate a security mode control procedure to take the new partial native 5G NAS security context into use, in order to avoid a KAUSF key mismatch between the UE and the network.

results.question: Following a successful 5G AKA primary authentication, what procedure must the AMF initiate and why is it initiated immediately?
results.reference: The AMF shall initiate a security mode control procedure to take the new partial native 5G NAS security context into use. It is initiated immediately to avoid KAUSF key mismatch between the UE and the network.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.1.3.1, General
results.model_answer:
Following a successful 5G AKA based primary authentication and key agreement procedure, the AMF **must initiate the NAS security mode control procedure** (per subclause 5.4.2) in order to **take the new partial native 5G NAS security context into use**.

**Why it must be initiated immediately:**

The AMF is required to initiate this security mode control procedure **immediately** after the successful 5G AKA primary authentication **to avoid a KAUSF key mismatch between the UE and the network**.

This urgency stems from a key behavior noted in the specification: generation of a new KAUSF (and new KSEAF) during a successful 5G AKA procedure **does not automatically delete the previously valid KAUSF and KSEAF**. This means that, at least temporarily, both the UE and the network could have two sets of keys (the old valid ones and the new ones just generated). If the security mode control procedure is delayed, there is a risk that the UE and the network could become desynchronized regarding which KAUSF (and associated KSEAF) is considered "valid" — i.e., a mismatch could arise if one side continues operating with the old context while the other has moved to the new one, or if ambiguity exists regarding which context is authoritative.

By immediately triggering the security mode control procedure, the AMF ensures that:
1. The new partial native 5G NAS security context (established via the successful primary authentication) is promptly activated.
2. Upon the UE's acceptance of the SECURITY MODE COMMAND, the ME explicitly **deletes the old valid KAUSF and KSEAF** (if any) and **designates the new KAUSF and KSEAF as valid**, resetting associated counters (SOR counter, UE parameter update counter) accordingly.

This immediate transition eliminates the window of ambiguity between old and new key material, ensuring both UE and network are synchronized on a single, consistent security context going forward.

results.question: How does the AMF initiate the network slice-specific EAP message reliable transport procedure?
results.reference: The AMF creates a NETWORK SLICE-SPECIFIC AUTHENTICATION COMMAND message, sets the EAP message IE to the EAP-request message (generated by AMF or from AAA-S via NSSAAF), sets the S-NSSAI IE to the relevant HPLMN or SNPN S-NSSAI, sends the message, and starts timer T3575 per S-NSSAI.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.7.2.1, Network slice-specific EAP message reliable transport procedure initiation
results.model_answer:
Based on Clause 5.4.7.2.1, the AMF initiates the **network slice-specific EAP message reliable transport procedure** by performing the following steps:

1. **Create the message**: The AMF creates a **NETWORK SLICE-SPECIFIC AUTHENTICATION COMMAND** message.

2. **Set the EAP message IE**: The AMF sets the EAP message IE of this message to the **EAP-request message**, which is either:
   - generated by the AMF itself, or
   - provided by the AAA-S via the NSSAAF.

3. **Set the S-NSSAI IE**: The AMF sets the S-NSSAI IE of this message to the **HPLMN S-NSSAI or the SNPN S-NSSAI** to which the EAP-request message is related.

4. **Send the message and start the timer**: The AMF sends the NETWORK SLICE-SPECIFIC AUTHENTICATION COMMAND message and **starts timer T3575 per S-NSSAI**.

In summary, the AMF builds a NETWORK SLICE-SPECIFIC AUTHENTICATION COMMAND message carrying the EAP-request message and its associated S-NSSAI, sends it to the UE, and starts timer T3575 (tracked per S-NSSAI) to await the UE's response.
results.evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.7.2.1, Network slice-specific EAP message reliable transport procedure initiation

results.question: What two pieces of information does the UE pass to its upper layers upon receiving a NETWORK SLICE-SPECIFIC AUTHENTICATION COMMAND message?
results.reference: The UE passes the EAP-request message from the EAP message IE and the HPLMN S-NSSAI or SNPN S-NSSAI from the S-NSSAI IE to the upper layers.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.7.2.1, Network slice-specific EAP message reliable transport procedure initiation
results.model_answer:
Upon receiving a NETWORK SLICE-SPECIFIC AUTHENTICATION COMMAND message, the UE passes the following two pieces of information to the upper layers:

a) **The EAP-request message** received in the EAP message IE; and

b) **The HPLMN S-NSSAI or the SNPN S-NSSAI** received in the S-NSSAI IE.

(Note: Before performing this action, the UE also stops timer T3346 if it is running, but this is a separate action from the information passed to the upper layers. Apart from passing this information to the upper layers, the procedure remains transparent to the UE's 5GMM layer.)

results.question: What is the role of the S-NSSAI IE in the NETWORK SLICE-SPECIFIC AUTHENTICATION COMMAND message during procedure initiation?
results.reference: The S-NSSAI IE is set by the AMF to the HPLMN S-NSSAI or the SNPN S-NSSAI to which the EAP-request message is related, identifying the specific network slice for the authentication.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.7.2.1, Network slice-specific EAP message reliable transport procedure initiation
results.model_answer:
The S-NSSAI IE identifies **which network slice (HPLMN S-NSSAI or SNPN S-NSSAI) the carried EAP-request message relates to**.

Specifically, during initiation of the network slice-specific EAP message reliable transport procedure (Clause 5.4.7.2.1):

- The AMF sets the S-NSSAI IE to the **HPLMN S-NSSAI or the SNPN S-NSSAI to which the EAP-request message is related**. This ties the EAP-request (carried in the EAP message IE) to a specific slice, since network slice-specific authentication and authorization is performed per S-NSSAI.

- On the UE side, upon receiving the message, the UE **passes both the EAP-request message and the associated S-NSSAI (from the S-NSSAI IE) to the upper layers together**. This allows the upper layers to correctly associate the EAP-request with the correct S-NSSAI's stored credentials, since a UE may be undergoing NSSAA for multiple S-NSSAIs concurrently (each tracked independently, e.g., with T3575 started "per S-NSSAI").

- The S-NSSAI IE thus serves as a **correlation/addressing identifier**, ensuring the EAP signalling exchanged between the UE's upper layers and the AAA-S (via AMF/NSSAAF) is routed and matched to the correct ongoing per-slice authentication context, since the 5GMM layer itself treats the EAP content as transparent and relies on the S-NSSAI to disambiguate between parallel NSSAA procedures for different slices.

In short: the S-NSSAI IE binds the transported EAP-request to the specific slice-authentication instance it belongs to, enabling both the AMF (which manages T3575 per S-NSSAI) and the UE's upper layers to correctly correlate the message with the right ongoing NSSAA procedure.
results.evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.7.2.1, Network slice-specific EAP message reliable transport procedure initiation

results.question: What immediate action does the UE take regarding timers when it receives a NETWORK SLICE-SPECIFIC AUTHENTICATION COMMAND message?
results.reference: The UE stops timer T3346 if it is running, before passing the EAP-request and S-NSSAI to the upper layers.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.7.2.1, Network slice-specific EAP message reliable transport procedure initiation
results.model_answer: Upon receipt of a NETWORK SLICE-SPECIFIC AUTHENTICATION COMMAND message, the UE shall **stop timer T3346 if it is running**.

results.question: What is the purpose of the EAP message information element within the PDU SESSION AUTHENTICATION RESULT message in this procedure?
results.reference: To carry the final EAP packet (EAP Success or EAP Failure) that provides the result of the EAP authentication procedure, allowing the UE to report this result to the network.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.1.3, PDU EAP result message transport procedure
results.model_answer:
Based on clause 6.3.1.3.1, the **EAP message IE** within the PDU SESSION AUTHENTICATION RESULT message serves to carry the **EAP-success message provided by the DN** to the UE.

Specifically, its purpose is:

1. **Transport function**: It is the mechanism by which the SMF conveys the outcome of a successful DN authentication/authorization (that occurred *after* the PDU session was already established) back to the UE, since this EAP-success message cannot be piggybacked on a PDU SESSION ESTABLISHMENT ACCEPT message (as that procedure already completed).

2. **Content carried**: The SMF sets this IE specifically to the EAP-success message received from the DN—confirming that the DN authentication of the UE completed successfully.

3. **Delivery to upper layers**: Upon receipt of the PDU SESSION AUTHENTICATION RESULT message, the UE's 5GSM layer extracts the EAP message from this IE and passes it up to the upper layers (i.e., it does not process or interpret the EAP content itself).

4. **Transparency**: Aside from relaying this EAP message to upper layers, the entire authentication and authorization procedure initiated by the DN remains transparent to the UE's 5GSM layer — meaning the 5GSM layer has no other role in interpreting the EAP exchange; it is purely a transport conduit for the EAP-success indication between the DN (via SMF) and the UE's upper layers.

In essence, the EAP message IE's purpose here is **result notification and transparent relay**: it informs the UE (via its upper layers) that the post-establishment DN authentication succeeded, without requiring the 5GSM layer itself to interpret the EAP semantics.
results.evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.1.3.1, PDU EAP result message transport procedure initiation

results.question: What specific action must the SMF take regarding timer T3592 upon receiving an indication that N1 SM delivery was skipped, and under what condition does this apply?
results.reference: The SMF shall stop timer T3592. This applies when the PDU SESSION RELEASE COMMAND message was sent along the N1 SM delivery skip allowed indication towards AMF and the SMF receives an indication that N1 SM delivery was skipped.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.3.4, N1 SM delivery skipped
results.model_answer:
Based on Clause 6.3.3.4 (N1 SM delivery skipped), the SMF's action is as follows:

**Condition:**
This applies when the SMF has sent the **PDU SESSION RELEASE COMMAND** message **along with the N1 SM delivery skip allowed indication** towards the AMF (as part of the network-requested PDU session release procedure). Subsequently, the SMF receives an **indication from the AMF that N1 SM delivery was skipped** (i.e., the AMF did not forward the N1 SM container/PDU SESSION RELEASE COMMAND to the UE).

**Required Action:**
Upon receiving that indication, the SMF shall:
1. **Stop timer T3592** — this is the timer that was started when the SMF originally sent the PDU SESSION RELEASE COMMAND (as specified in Clause 6.3.3.2, the SMF starts T3592 upon sending the PDU SESSION RELEASE COMMAND together with the N1 SM delivery skip allowed indication).
2. **Consider the PDU session as released** — even though the UE never actually received the N1 SM container, the SMF treats the release as complete on the network side.

**Summary:**
The SMF stops T3592 and treats the PDU session as released, specifically triggered by (a) prior inclusion of the N1 SM delivery skip allowed indication in the PDU SESSION RELEASE COMMAND sent to the AMF, and (b) subsequent receipt of confirmation from the AMF that it indeed skipped delivering the N1 SM information to the UE. This effectively allows the SMF to finalize the release procedure without waiting for explicit UE acknowledgment, since the AMF's skip indication substitutes for the UE's response in this optimized signaling path.
results.evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.3.4, N1 SM delivery skipped

results.question: How should the SMF treat the state of the PDU session after receiving an indication of skipped N1 SM delivery following a specific message transmission?
results.reference: The SMF shall consider the PDU session as released. This occurs after the SMF sent the PDU SESSION RELEASE COMMAND message with the N1 SM delivery skip allowed indication and subsequently receives an indication that N1 SM delivery was skipped.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.3.4, N1 SM delivery skipped
results.model_answer:
Per clause 6.3.3.4 (N1 SM delivery skipped), if the SMF sent the **PDU SESSION RELEASE COMMAND** message together with the **N1 SM delivery skip allowed indication** to the AMF, then upon receiving an indication that the N1 SM delivery was skipped, the SMF shall:

1. **Stop timer T3592**, and
2. **Consider the PDU session as released.**

In other words, even though the UE never actually received the N1 SM container (since the AMF skipped forwarding it), the SMF treats the release as having taken effect — it does not wait for further confirmation or let T3592 expire, and immediately transitions the PDU session state to released on the network side.
results.evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.3.4, N1 SM delivery skipped

results.question: Describe the procedural consequence for the SMF when N1 SM delivery is skipped, given a prior transmission of the PDU SESSION RELEASE COMMAND message with a specific indication.
results.reference: The procedural consequence is twofold: the SMF shall stop timer T3592 and shall consider the PDU session as released. This is triggered by receiving an indication that N1 SM delivery was skipped, which follows the sending of the PDU SESSION RELEASE COMMAND message along the N1 SM delivery skip allowed indication towards the AMF.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.3.4, N1 SM delivery skipped
results.model_answer:
Based on Clause 6.3.3.4 (N1 SM delivery skipped), the procedural consequence for the SMF is as follows:

**Precondition:** The SMF must have previously sent the PDU SESSION RELEASE COMMAND message together with the **N1 SM delivery skip allowed indication** towards the AMF.

**Trigger:** The SMF subsequently receives an indication from the AMF that the N1 SM delivery (i.e., delivery of the N1 SM container/PDU SESSION RELEASE COMMAND to the UE) was skipped.

**Consequence for the SMF:**
1. The SMF **shall stop timer T3592** — this is the timer that was started when the SMF initially sent the PDU SESSION RELEASE COMMAND message (per Clause 6.3.3.2), and which would otherwise be used to await confirmation/retransmission handling for the release procedure.
2. The SMF **shall consider the PDU session as released** — even though the UE was never actually notified via N1 SM signalling that its session was released, the SMF treats the release procedure as having completed successfully.

**Rationale/Context:** This behavior is only permitted because the SMF had explicitly authorized the AMF to skip N1 SM delivery in the first place (via the N1 SM delivery skip allowed indication). That indication is itself conditioned on specific criteria from Clause 6.3.3.2 — namely, either:
- the AMF is allowed to skip sending the N1 SM container to the UE and the 5GSM cause IE is *not* set to #39 "reactivation requested"; or
- the AMF is allowed to skip sending the N1 SM container and the Access type IE is *not* included in the PDU SESSION RELEASE COMMAND.

In effect, the SMF pre-authorizes a "fire-and-forget" style release for cases where it does not matter (or is not critical) whether the UE explicitly received the release command, and upon confirmation that this skip occurred, it finalizes the session release locally without waiting further for T3592 to expire or for any UE acknowledgment.
results.evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.3.4, N1 SM delivery skipped

results.question: What two definitive steps must the SMF perform upon being informed that N1 SM delivery was skipped, and what is the prerequisite message context for these steps?
results.reference: The SMF must stop timer T3592 and consider the PDU session as released. The prerequisite is that the SMF had previously sent the PDU SESSION RELEASE COMMAND message along the N1 SM delivery skip allowed indication towards the AMF.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.3.4, N1 SM delivery skipped
results.model_answer:
Based on Clause 6.3.3.4, when the SMF receives an indication that N1 SM delivery was skipped, it must perform two definitive steps:

**Prerequisite message context:**
The PDU SESSION RELEASE COMMAND message must have been sent **along with the N1 SM delivery skip allowed indication** towards the AMF. This is a mandatory precondition — the SMF's subsequent actions upon receiving the "skipped" indication only apply if this indication was included in the original message to the AMF.

**The two definitive steps the SMF must perform:**

1. **Stop timer T3592** — The SMF stops the timer that was started when the PDU SESSION RELEASE COMMAND message (with the N1 SM delivery skip allowed indication) was sent to the AMF, as specified in the network-requested PDU session release procedure initiation (Clause 6.3.3.2).

2. **Consider the PDU session as released** — The SMF treats the PDU session as if the release procedure has completed successfully, even though the AMF did not actually deliver the N1 SM container (i.e., the PDU SESSION RELEASE COMMAND payload) to the UE.

**Underlying logic:**
This behavior reflects the design intent behind the N1 SM delivery skip allowed indication described in Clause 6.3.3.2: the SMF explicitly permits the AMF to skip forwarding the N1 SM container to the UE under certain conditions (e.g., when the 5GSM cause is not #39 "reactivation requested," or when the Access type IE is not included). Since the SMF has already authorized this skip, receiving confirmation that the AMF exercised this option is sufficient for the SMF to finalize the release locally — without waiting for explicit UE acknowledgment via the N1 SM container — thereby avoiding unnecessary timer expiry (T3592) and redundant release signaling.
results.evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 6.3.3.4, N1 SM delivery skipped

results.question: How does a UE in 5GMM-CONNECTED mode with RRC inactive indication process an access attempt upon detecting one of the events listed in subclause 4.5.1?
results.reference: The NAS categorizes the access attempt into access identities and an access category using either the standard tables and procedures (if not in SNPN mode) or the SNPN-specific tables and procedures (if in SNPN mode), and provides these to the lower layers for access control checking.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.5.4.2, Access control and checking in 5GMM-CONNECTED mode and in 5GMM-CONNECTED mode with RRC inactive indication
results.model_answer:
Based on subclause 4.5.4.2, when a UE in **5GMM-CONNECTED mode with RRC inactive indication** detects one of events 1) through 8) listed in subclause 4.5.1, it processes the access attempt as follows:

## 1. Categorization of the Access Attempt

The NAS shall categorize the access attempt into **access identities** and an **access category**, following:
- **a)** Subclause 4.5.2, Table 4.5.2.1 and Table 4.5.2.2, and subclause 4.5.3 — if the UE is **not** operating in SNPN access mode; or
- **b)** Subclause 4.5.2A, Table 4.5.2A.1 and Table 4.5.2A.2, and subclause 4.5.3 — if the UE **is** operating in SNPN access mode

## 2. Providing Information to Lower Layers

The NAS provides the **access identities** and **access category** to the lower layers for access control checking purposes. The NAS may also provide the **RRC establishment cause** (determined per subclause 4.5.6) in this same request.

> **Note:** As an implementation option, the NAS can defer providing the RRC establishment cause until after being informed that the access attempt is allowed.

## 3. Uplink Data Status Handling

If the UE has uplink user data pending for one or more PDU sessions when building a REGISTRATION REQUEST or SERVICE REQUEST message, it **shall** indicate the respective PDU sessions in the **Uplink data status IE**, regardless of the access category being checked (i.e., even if barring timers are running for other categories).

## 4. Action Based on Lower Layer Response

**If access is allowed**, the NAS proceeds according to the triggering event, e.g.:
- MO-IMS/MMTEL/SMSoIP indications → notify upper layers that access is allowed
- MO SMS request → initiate NAS transport procedure (subclause 5.4.5)
- New/modified PDU session request → initiate NAS transport procedure for ESTABLISHMENT/MODIFICATION REQUEST
- User-plane re-establishment request → initiate service request procedure (subclause 5.6.1)
- Suspended UP data packet → consider it allowed to send
- MO location request → send LCS message via UL NAS TRANSPORT
- UE policy container transaction → send via UL NAS TRANSPORT

**If access is barred**, the NAS **does not** initiate the corresponding procedure/message, and instead:
- For IMS-related indications: notifies upper layers of barring (dual-registration UEs may fall back to S1 mode)
- For other events (SMS, PDU session establishment/modification, re-establishment, LCS, UE policy container): NAS withholds the corresponding message/procedure, and **may** initiate it later, if still needed, upon receiving an indication from lower layers that barring is alleviated for that access category
- For suspended UP data packets specifically: NAS **shall** consider the barring alleviated once indicated (mandatory re-attempt, not just "may")

results.question: What additional information can the NAS provide to the lower layers alongside the access identities and category when requesting access control checking for an event in connected mode?
results.reference: In the request to the lower layer, the NAS can also provide the RRC establishment cause determined as specified in subclause 4.5.6.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.5.4.2, Access control and checking in 5GMM-CONNECTED mode and in 5GMM-CONNECTED mode with RRC inactive indication
results.model_answer:
The NAS can additionally provide the **RRC establishment cause**, determined as specified in subclause 4.5.6, to the lower layers along with the access identities and access category in the access control checking request.

Note (as per NOTE1 in clause 4.5.4.2): as an implementation option, the NAS can choose to provide this RRC establishment cause to the lower layers **after** being informed by the lower layers that the access attempt is allowed, rather than providing it upfront together with the access identities and access category.
results.evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.5.4.1, Access control and checking in 5GMM-IDLE mode and in 5GMM-IDLE mode with suspend indication

results.question: How does the UE handle a request from upper layers to send a mobile originated location request when access control bars the associated access attempt in connected mode?
results.reference: The 5GMM shall not initiate the NAS transport procedure to send the LCS message. It may initiate the procedure later if the lower layers indicate the barring is alleviated for that access category and the message is still needed.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.5.4.2, Access control and checking in 5GMM-CONNECTED mode and in 5GMM-CONNECTED mode with RRC inactive indication
results.model_answer:
When the UE is in 5GMM-CONNECTED mode or 5GMM-CONNECTED mode with RRC inactive indication and the lower layers indicate that the access attempt for the mobile originated location request is barred, 5GMM shall **not** initiate the NAS transport procedure (per subclause 5.4.5) to send the LCS message in an UL NAS TRANSPORT message.

Subsequently, upon receiving an indication from the lower layers that the barring is alleviated for the access category associated with that access attempt, 5GMM **may** initiate the NAS transport procedure (per subclause 5.4.5) to send the LCS message in an UL NAS TRANSPORT message, **if still needed**.

results.question: During which procedure may the T3502 value IE be provided?
results.reference: During the initial registration procedure.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.9.3, T3502 value
results.model_answer:
Based on the context provided (clauses [1] and [4], both titled "T3502 value"), the T3502 value IE **may be included to indicate a value for timer T3502 during the initial registration** procedure.

This is consistent with clause [2]/[3] (Handling of timer T3502), which specifies:
- T3502 can be sent in the **REGISTRATION ACCEPT** message (for the assigned registration area, applicable in all tracking areas until a new value is received), or
- T3502 can be sent in the **REGISTRATION REJECT** message **specifically during the initial registration** procedure.

By contrast, clauses [5] and [6] show a more generic wording ("may be included to indicate a value for timer T3502" without restricting it to "during the initial registration"), suggesting that this broader form applies to the REGISTRATION ACCEPT message case, which is not limited to initial registration alone but applies whenever the network assigns a registration area (including mobility/periodic registration updates).

**Summary:**
The T3502 value IE may be provided by the network:
- In the **REGISTRATION ACCEPT** message (general case, clause 8.2.7.18) — applicable to initial registration, mobility registration update, or periodic registration update procedures.
- In the **REGISTRATION REJECT** message (clause 8.2.9.3), but **only during the initial registration** procedure.

results.question: How does the network communicate a specific T3502 timer value to the UE?
results.reference: By including the T3502 value information element in a message during initial registration.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.9.3, T3502 value
results.model_answer:
The network communicates a specific value for timer **T3502** to the UE via NAS signalling messages during registration, specifically:

1. **REGISTRATION ACCEPT message** – The network can include a T3502 value in this message, which is sent upon successful completion of a registration procedure. The UE shall apply this received value in all tracking areas of the assigned registration area, until a new value is received.

2. **REGISTRATION REJECT message (during initial registration only)** – The network can also include a T3502 value in this message. However, this value is only adopted by the UE **if the REGISTRATION REJECT message was received integrity protected**. In that case, the UE applies this value until a new value is received with integrity protection, or until a new PLMN is selected. If the message was **not** integrity protected, the UE disregards the provided value and falls back to the default value of the timer.

**Corresponding IE details** (per the referenced clauses 8.2.9.3 and 8.2.7.18):
- The **T3502 value IE** may be included in the REGISTRATION ACCEPT message to indicate a value for T3502 (usable more generally).
- The **T3502 value IE** may also be included specifically **during the initial registration** context (i.e., in REGISTRATION REJECT) to indicate a value for T3502.

**Summary:** The network signals the T3502 value by embedding the optional T3502 value IE within either a REGISTRATION ACCEPT message (any registration outcome) or a REGISTRATION REJECT message (only during initial registration, and only effective if integrity protected). If no such IE is included, or the conditions for accepting a REGISTRATION REJECT-provided value are not met, the UE reverts to using the default T3502 value.
results.evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.3.8, Handling of timer T3502

results.question: How does the independence of 5GMM state machine instances between 3GPP and non-3GPP access impact UE registration status?
results.reference: The registration status and 5GMM parameters of the UE's 3GPP access and non-3GPP access 5GMM state machine instances are independent and can be different in each access.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 4.7.2.1, General
results.model_answer:
Based on clause 4.7.2.1 (item a), the UE maintains two entirely separate 5GMM state machine instances — one for 3GPP access and one for non-3GPP access. This independence has several concrete impacts on registration status:

## 1. Independent Registration Status
The UE can be registered on one access while deregistered on the other. For example, a UE could be in **5GMM-REGISTERED** over 3GPP access while remaining **5GMM-DEREGISTERED** over non-3GPP access (or vice versa). There is no requirement that registration on one access implies or triggers registration on the other.

## 2. Independent 5GMM Parameters
Since the state machines are independent, associated parameters can differ per access, including:
- **RPLMN**: The RPLMN over non-3GPP access can differ from the RPLMN over 3GPP access — even the MCC can differ (item c).
- **5G-GUTI, TAI list, ngKSI, 5GS update status**: These are tracked and deleted/reset separately per access, as seen throughout the cause-code handling in clause 5.5.2.3.4/5.3.20.2 (e.g., "delete 5G-GUTI... for non-3GPP access" vs "...for 3GPP access").
- **Registration attempt counters**: Separate counters exist for 3GPP and non-3GPP access (clause 5.5.1.1/5.3.20.2), and resetting one does not reset the other (e.g., NOTE2 confirms EPS attach only resets the 3GPP access counter).

## 3. No Single/Dual-Registration Mode Coupling
Item (b) confirms that single-registration/dual-registration mode concepts (which govern EPS/5GS interworking) do not apply to non-3GPP access — reinforcing that non-3GPP registration state is not coupled to any other access's state machine.

## 4. Separate Registration Procedures Required
Item (d) states registration for 3GPP and non-3GPP access is performed **separately**, with independent registration areas (each associated with a single TAI). A UE must explicitly register over each access; success or failure on one access does not automatically alter registration status on the other.

## 5. Independent Failure/Reject Handling
As seen in the cause-code procedures (e.g., #72, #73, #74-#78), a reject received over one access type generally affects only that access's 5GMM state, GUTI, TAI list, and update status — the other access's registration remains unaffected unless the UE, as an implementation option, chooses to also attempt or adjust the other access (explicitly called out as optional behavior, not mandatory coupling).

## 6. Practical Consequence
This independence means a UE can simultaneously have **two different registration states, two different RPLMNs, and two different sets of stored 5GMM parameters** — enabling multi-access registration scenarios (e.g., N3IWF connection independent of 3GPP RAN state) without cross-access state contamination, except where explicitly cross-referenced (e.g., cause #27 disables N1 mode capability for *both* accesses, or cause #72/#73 may optionally trigger action on the other access).

results.question: Under what specific access condition is the Forbidden TAI(s) for the list of '5GS forbidden tracking areas for roaming' IE included in a message?

results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.9.11, Forbidden TAI(s) for the list of "5GS forbidden tracking areas for roaming"
results.model_answer: The IE is included **only if the message is sent via satellite NG-RAN access**.
results.evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.7.48, Forbidden TAI(s) for the list of "5GS forbidden tracking areas for roaming"

results.question: What is the purpose of including the Forbidden TAI(s) IE for the list of '5GS forbidden tracking areas for roaming'?
results.reference: To indicate the forbidden tracking area identities that should be stored in the list of '5GS forbidden tracking areas for roaming'.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.9.11, Forbidden TAI(s) for the list of "5GS forbidden tracking areas for roaming"
results.model_answer:
The **Forbidden TAI(s) IE** is included so that the network can explicitly signal to the UE which TAI(s) should be added to (stored in) the UE's **list of "5GS forbidden tracking areas for roaming."**

Key points on its purpose and applicability:

- **Function**: It carries the specific TAI(s) that the UE must store in the "5GS forbidden tracking areas for roaming" list, per clause 5.3.13.
- **Conditional inclusion**: This IE is only included when the message is sent **via satellite NG-RAN access**. Over terrestrial NG-RAN access, this explicit signaling is not needed, presumably because the UE's serving TAI is unambiguous and forbidden-area handling relies on reject causes (e.g., #13 "roaming not allowed in this tracking area") rather than explicit TAI lists.
- **Rationale tied to satellite access**: As described in clause 4.23.5/5.3.13 context, a UE camping on a satellite NG-RAN cell may receive **multiple TACs** from the lower layers simultaneously (since a single satellite beam/cell can span multiple tracking areas). This creates ambiguity as to which TAI the network's rejection or acceptance actually pertains to. By including the Forbidden TAI(s) IE, the network can **explicitly identify which of the multiple candidate TAIs** (constructed by the UE from the multiple received TACs) should be marked as forbidden for roaming, rather than relying on the UE to infer this from a single ambiguous "current TAI."
- **Usage context**: This IE appears in relevant 5GMM messages (e.g., REGISTRATION REJECT/ACCEPT, SERVICE REJECT/ACCEPT, DEREGISTRATION REQUEST — corresponding to the various clauses 8.2.7, 8.2.9, 8.2.14, 8.2.17, 8.2.18) so that whenever the network rejects or restricts service with a roaming-related cause over satellite access, it can unambiguously convey the affected TAI(s) for the UE to add to its forbidden list, supporting correct TAI selection logic as described in clause 4.23.5 (e.g., avoiding reselection of a TAI that is in the forbidden list).

In short: **the IE's purpose is to let the network unambiguously specify, in satellite NG-RAN scenarios where multiple TACs/TAIs may be present at once, exactly which TAI(s) the UE should record as forbidden for roaming**, ensuring correct UE behavior in TAI selection and preventing the UE from treating a forbidden TAI as usable.

results.question: In which list are the TAI(s) indicated by the Forbidden TAI(s) IE intended to be stored?
results.reference: The TAI(s) are to be stored in the list of '5GS forbidden tracking areas for roaming'.

results.model_answer: The TAI(s) indicated by the "Forbidden TAI(s)" IE are intended to be stored in the **"5GS forbidden tracking areas for roaming"** list (or, for the separate IE at [8], the **"5GS forbidden tracking areas for regional provision of service"** list), depending on which specific IE is used. Both IEs are included only when the message is sent via satellite NG-RAN access.

results.question: How does the access type determine the inclusion of the Forbidden TAI(s) IE for the '5GS forbidden tracking areas for roaming' list?
results.reference: The IE is included only if the message is transmitted specifically via satellite NG-RAN access; it is not included for other access types.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.9.11, Forbidden TAI(s) for the list of "5GS forbidden tracking areas for roaming"
results.model_answer:
Based on the context [3]–[7], the **Forbidden TAI(s) for the list of "5GS forbidden tracking areas for roaming"** IE is conditionally included depending on the **access type** used to deliver the NAS message:

- **Included**: The IE is included **only if the message is sent via satellite NG-RAN access**. This applies uniformly across all the referenced clauses (8.2.7.48, 8.2.9.11, 8.2.17.8, 8.2.14.9, 8.2.18.10), regardless of which specific NAS message carries the IE (e.g., REGISTRATION ACCEPT, SERVICE ACCEPT, etc., as implied by clause 5.3.13's reference to messages carrying forbidden TAI(s)).

- **Not included**: If the message is sent via **any other access type** — i.e., non-satellite 3GPP access (terrestrial NG-RAN), wireline access, or non-3GPP access (trusted/untrusted) — the IE is **not included**.

**Rationale inferred from context:**

1. Clause [1]/[2] explains that over 3GPP access, the network can directly signal forbidden TAI(s) to the UE via REGISTRATION ACCEPT or SERVICE ACCEPT messages (in addition to reject-cause-triggered updates). This IE is the mechanism by which the network explicitly delivers TAI(s) to be added to the forbidden list.

2. The restriction to **satellite NG-RAN access** aligns with the special complexity introduced in [8]: satellite NG-RAN cells can broadcast **multiple TACs** simultaneously (unlike terrestrial cells, which typically broadcast a single TAC). This creates ambiguity — the network cannot rely on the UE unambiguously deriving which TAI(s) are forbidden from cell broadcast alone, since a satellite cell may span TAIs that mix allowed/forbidden status.

3. Therefore, for satellite NG-RAN access, the network uses this IE to **explicitly and unambiguously indicate** which TAI(s) (among the multiple TACs the UE may encounter) should be added to the forbidden list, ensuring correct list population despite the multi-TAC satellite scenario.

4. For terrestrial 3GPP access, wireline access, and non-3GPP access, no such ambiguity exists (single TAC per cell, or as noted in [1]'s NOTE, non-3GPP access doesn't maintain TAI-based forbidden lists at all), so explicit IE-based signaling of forbidden TAIs is unnecessary — the UE can rely on the existing mechanisms (TAI list receipt, reject causes) described in clause 5.3.13 to manage the list.

**Summary:** Access type determines inclusion in a binary fashion — the IE is present *only* for satellite NG-RAN access, and absent for all other access types (terrestrial 3GPP, wireline, non-3GPP), because only satellite access introduces the multi-TAC ambiguity that necessitates explicit forbidden TAI signaling from the network.

results.question: What actions must the AMF take regarding timer T3555 upon receiving a CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMPLETE message?
results.reference: The AMF must stop timer T3555 when it receives the CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMPLETE message.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.4.4, Generic UE configuration update completion by the network
results.model_answer: Upon receipt of the CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMPLETE message, the AMF shall **stop timer T3555**.

results.question: How does the AMF handle a new 5G-GUTI and TAI list received in a CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMMAND message after the UE sends CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMPLETE?
results.reference: The AMF considers the new 5G-GUTI as valid and the old 5G-GUTI as invalid, and similarly considers the new TAI list as valid and the old TAI list as invalid.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.4.4, Generic UE configuration update completion by the network
results.model_answer:
Based on clause 5.4.4.4 (Generic UE configuration update completion by the network):

Upon receipt of the **CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMPLETE** message, the AMF shall:

1. **Stop timer T3555**

2. **5G-GUTI handling**: If a new 5G-GUTI was included in the CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMMAND message, the AMF shall consider the **new 5G-GUTI as valid** and the **old 5G-GUTI as invalid**.

3. **TAI list handling**: If a new TAI list was included in the CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMMAND message, the AMF shall consider the **new TAI list as valid** and the **old TAI list as invalid**.

In essence, successful receipt of the CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMPLETE message serves as confirmation that the UE has successfully received and applied the new identity/mobility parameters, so the AMF immediately finalizes the transition — invalidating the old 5G-GUTI and old TAI list at that point, rather than maintaining the dual-validity period described in the abnormal-case handling (clause 5.4.4.6) for lower-layer failure scenarios, where both old and new values must be kept valid until the old ones can safely be considered invalid.

This contrasts with the **lower layer failure** case (5.4.4.6, case b-1), where the CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMPLETE is *not* received — in that situation, both old and new 5G-GUTIs (and TAI lists, and Paging subgroup IDs, if applicable) must be considered valid simultaneously until the network can confirm which one the UE is actually using, via paging responses or a subsequent identification/configuration update procedure.

results.question: What is the AMF's procedure when a new T3447 value is included in the CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMMAND message and the UE completes the update?
results.reference: The AMF considers the T3447 value as valid. If the value is neither zero nor indicates deactivation, it uses this value the next time timer T3447 is started. If the value indicates deactivation or is zero, the AMF stops timer T3447 if it is running.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.4.4, Generic UE configuration update completion by the network
results.model_answer:
Based on Clause 5.4.4.4, upon receipt of the CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMPLETE message (i.e., after the UE completes the configuration update), the AMF handles the T3447 value as follows:

- If a T3447 value was included in the CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMMAND message, the AMF shall **consider the T3447 value as valid**, and **if the value is neither zero nor deactivated**, the AMF shall **use this new T3447 value the next time timer T3447 is started**.

- If instead the T3447 value included in the CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMMAND message **indicated that the timer is deactivated or set to zero**, then the AMF shall **stop timer T3447 if it is currently running**.

In summary: the AMF adopts the new T3447 value as valid, applying it on the next start of T3447 (unless the value signals deactivation/zero, in which case any running T3447 is stopped instead).
results.evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.4.4, Generic UE configuration update completion by the network

results.question: Under what condition regarding LADN information does the AMF indicate UE presence in LADN service area to the SMF after a configuration update?
results.reference: The AMF indicates UE presence in LADN service area to the SMF if the tracking area identity list in the new LADN information does not include the current TA.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 5.4.4.4, Generic UE configuration update completion by the network
results.model_answer:
Based on clause 5.4.4.4, when a **LADN information IE** is included in the CONFIGURATION UPDATE COMMAND message, the AMF replaces the old LADN information with the new LADN information as valid. 

The specific condition triggering the AMF to indicate **UE presence in LADN service area** to the SMF is:

**If the tracking area identity (TAI) list in the new LADN information does not include the current TA (Tracking Area) that the UE is currently located in.**

In other words, the AMF checks whether the UE's current TA falls within the LADN service area defined by the newly received LADN information. If the current TA is **not** part of the TAI list included in the new LADN information (meaning the UE is now considered outside the LADN service area based on the updated information), the AMF must indicate this UE presence status (i.e., that the UE is outside the LADN service area) to the SMF, as specified in 3GPP TS 23.501 and TS 23.502.

results.question: How does the UE behave when it is in the 5GMM-NULL state regarding the initiation of 5GMM procedures?
results.reference: The UE shall not initiate any 5GMM procedures when in the 5GMM-NULL state.
results.model_answer: Based on clause 5.1.3.2.1.2.1 (5GMM-NULL), when the UE is in this state, **5GS services are disabled in the UE**, and as a result, **no 5GS mobility management function shall be performed** in this state. This means the UE does not initiate any 5GMM procedures (such as registration, service request, or de-registration) while in the 5GMM-NULL state, since the 5GMM sublayer is effectively inactive.

results.question: Why is the 5GMM-NULL state considered the initial state for a UE's 5GMM mobility management?
results.reference: The 5GMM-NULL state is the initial state because the UE enters this state when it is switched on or when the USIM is inserted, before any registration procedure is initiated.
results.model_answer:
5GMM-NULL is the natural starting point because, in that state, **5GS services are disabled in the UE and no 5GMM procedures are performed at all** ([1]). This means the UE has not yet engaged the 5GMM sublayer in any capacity — it has not established a 5GMM context, it has not attempted registration, and it is not tracked by the network in any way.

This makes it fundamentally different from 5GMM-DEREGISTERED, which is the next state up: in DEREGISTERED, the UE is *capable* of performing mobility management (e.g., it can start an initial registration procedure), even though no context currently exists. 5GMM-NULL, by contrast, represents a state where the 5GMM sublayer is effectively inactive — analogous to the UE being powered off, having 5GS services disabled by the USIM/ME, or not yet having any USIM inserted. Since no mobility management function can be performed while in NULL, it logically precedes even DEREGISTERED, serving as the "no 5GMM entity exists yet" baseline from which the UE must transition (e.g., upon power-on or enabling 5GS services) before any registration attempt — and therefore before entering DEREGISTERED — can occur.

Supporting evidence from [5]/[6] reinforces this ordering: when describing conditions where "the UE is considered neither registered nor attached over 3GPP access," the specification explicitly lists the 5GMM-NULL state alongside 5GMM-DEREGISTERED and 5GMM-DEREGISTERED-INITIATED as states where no active 5GMM context exists — with NULL representing the most basic, pre-functional condition of all main states, since it's the only one in which 5GMM mobility management operation is entirely disabled rather than merely "not yet established."

results.question: What condition triggers a UE to transition from the 5GMM-NULL state to another 5GMM state?
results.reference: The UE leaves the 5GMM-NULL state and enters the 5GMM-DEREGISTERED state when it initiates the initial registration procedure.
results.model_answer:
Based on clause 5.2.2.3.7 (eCALL-INACTIVE substate description in [7]/[8]), a UE in **5GMM-NULL** transitions to another 5GMM state when it is **activated (e.g., powered on) by the user**.

This is inferred from the reverse condition explicitly stated: the UE leaves the eCALL-INACTIVE substate and **enters** 5GMM-NULL "if the UE is deactivated (e.g. powered off) by the user." Since 5GMM-NULL represents the state where "5GS services are disabled in the UE" and "no 5GS mobility management function shall be performed" (clause 5.1.3.2.1.2.1), the logical counterpart trigger for leaving 5GMM-NULL is the user powering on/activating the UE, causing 5GS services to be enabled and the UE to enter 5GMM-DEREGISTERED (or an appropriate substate) so that mobility management functions can begin.

results.question: How does the network's knowledge of the UE differ when the UE is in the 5GMM-NULL state compared to other states?
results.reference: In the 5GMM-NULL state, the network has no knowledge of the UE's location or its 5GMM context, as the UE has not yet performed any registration.
results.model_answer:
Based on Clause [1] (§5.1.3.2.1.2), the difference lies in how "unknown/unreachable" is characterized:

**5GMM-NULL:**
5GS services are disabled in the UE entirely, and no 5GMM function is performed. The clause does not describe this state in terms of network "knowledge" of the UE at all — there is no 5GMM context, and the concept of network awareness is essentially moot because the UE is not engaging in 5GS mobility management in any capacity. This is a more fundamental absence than "unknown location" — it reflects that 5GS is switched off from the UE's perspective.

**5GMM-DEREGISTERED (contrast case):**
Here, the text explicitly states: "no 5GMM context has been established **and the UE location is unknown to the network and hence it is unreachable by a network**." This is a state where 5GS services are still enabled/available to the UE, but no context has yet been (or is currently) established — the UE is a known concept to the network as a class of subscriber, but its specific location/context is not tracked.

**Other states (REGISTERED, REGISTERED-INITIATED, DEREGISTERED-INITIATED, SERVICE-REQUEST-INITIATED):**
In these states, a 5GMM context exists or is in the process of being established/removed, meaning the network has some level of knowledge/tracking of the UE (context, location awareness via TAI list, reachability, etc., depending on CM state).

**Key inferred distinction:**
The clause's explicit "unknown to the network... unreachable" language is tied specifically to 5GMM-DEREGISTERED, where the *absence of a 5GMM context* is the defining reason for unreachability. In 5GMM-NULL, no such statement is made because the state falls outside the scope of 5GMM entirely — the network's "knowledge" concept doesn't apply since the UE is not performing any 5GS mobility management and effectively does not exist as an active 5GS entity to the network at all. Thus 5GMM-NULL represents a total absence of 5GS engagement, whereas 5GMM-DEREGISTERED (and implicitly the other listed states, which build on an established or transitioning 5GMM context) represents a UE that is still within the 5GS mobility management framework, merely lacking (or negotiating) a context and associated location knowledge.

results.question: Under what condition might the network include the local time zone information element during a procedure?
results.reference: To assign a new local time zone to the UE.
results.gold_evidence: TS 24.501, Clause 8.2.19.9, Local time zone
results.model_answer:
The **Local time zone IE** may be included when the network wants to **assign a new local time zone value to the UE**.

In practice, this occurs as part of the **generic UE configuration update procedure** described in clause 5.4.4.1, where the AMF updates access and mobility management-related parameters for the UE. Specifically, "Network identity and time zone information" — which encompasses the local time zone (along with full/short network name, universal time and local time zone, and network daylight saving time) — is one of the parameters that:

- Can be sent to the UE **without requiring** the UE to perform a registration procedure for mobility and periodic registration update (i.e., it can be delivered directly via the UE Configuration Update Command); and
- Is managed **per access type** if the UE is not registered to the same PLMN/SNPN over both 3GPP and non-3GPP access, or managed **commonly** (sent over either access) if the UE is registered to the same PLMN/SNPN over both accesses.

So, the network includes the Local time zone IE whenever it needs to inform/update the UE with a new local time zone applicable to the network the UE is currently registered with — this is typically triggered by a change in the serving network's local time zone (e.g., due to mobility into a different time zone region or a daylight saving transition), and it is conveyed as part of the "Network identity and time zone information" parameter set within the UE Configuration Update Command.

results.question: What is the purpose of the local time zone IE as defined in the clause?
